"""Make every results figure (figures/fig*.png) for the project write-up.

Run:  python3 make_figures.py      (~1-2 min with numba)
All model checks use held-out seeds the calibration never saw.
Colors (validated colorblind-safe): S&P/real data = ink, calibrated = blue,
paper settings = orange, no chartists = aqua, references = muted gray dashes.
"""
from multiprocessing import Pool

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

from herding import calibrate, kirman, market_data, model, stats

FIG = market_data.ROOT / "figures"
INK, SECOND, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9"
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, RED = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#e34948"
BLUE_LIGHT = "#b7d3f6"
DAYS, BURN = 19300, 300
HELD_OUT = range(600, 620)                       # never used by the calibration
LABELS = dict(alpha_5pct="tail exponent α (5% tail)", alpha_1pct="tail exponent α (1% tail)",
              share_4sd="share of days beyond 4 std", ac_r_1="return correlation, 1 day",
              ac_r_2="return correlation, 2 days", ac_r_2to10="return correlation, days 2-10",
              ac_abs_1="volatility memory, 1 day", ac_abs_20="volatility memory, 20 days",
              ac_abs_50="volatility memory, 50 days", ac_abs_100="volatility memory, 100 days")

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 10, "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.titleweight": "bold", "axes.edgecolor": "#c3c2b7", "axes.labelcolor": SECOND,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
    "grid.linewidth": 0.6, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "legend.frameon": False,
    "lines.linewidth": 2, "savefig.dpi": 150, "savefig.bbox": "tight"})


def save(fig, name, caption):
    fig.text(0.01, -0.02, caption, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=SECOND, wrap=True)
    fig.savefig(FIG / name)
    plt.close(fig)
    print("saved", name)


def _run(args):
    p, seed, days, herding = args
    return model.simulate(days + BURN, herding, p, seed=seed)[0][BURN:]


def ensemble(pool, p, seeds=HELD_OUT, days=DAYS, herding=True):
    return pool.map(_run, [(p, s, days, herding) for s in seeds])


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 1
def fig_fingerprint(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
    target = stats.stylized_facts(spx)
    cal = [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in cal_runs]
    paper = [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in paper_runs]
    pct = calibrate.percentiles(target, cal, calibrate.TARGETS)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(15, 5.6))
    for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, calibrate.TARGETS):
        v = np.array([f[k] for f in cal])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95])
        ax.plot([0, 0], [lo, hi], color=BLUE, lw=6, solid_capstyle="round", alpha=0.35)
        ax.plot(0, med, "o", color=BLUE, ms=8, label="calibrated model (median, 5-95%)")
        ax.plot(0.25, np.median([f[k] for f in paper]), "X", color=ORANGE, ms=9,
                label="paper settings (median)")
        ax.plot(-0.25, target[k], "D", color=INK, ms=8, label="S&P 500 1950-2026")
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 0.6); ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_title(LABELS[k], fontsize=9.5)
        flag = "typical" if 5 <= pct[k] <= 95 else "UNUSUAL"
        ax.text(0.5, 0.02, f"S&P percentile {pct[k]:.0f}% ({flag})", transform=ax.transAxes,
                ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK if flag == "typical" else RED)
    h, l = axes.flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(h, l, loc="upper center", ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.04))
    fig.suptitle("Fig 1. The S&P 500's fingerprint vs 20 held-out histories of the calibrated model",
                 y=1.10, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    n_typ = sum(5 <= v <= 95 for v in pct.values())
    save(fig, "fig1_fingerprint.png",
         f"Each panel is one measure. Blue bar: the range covering 90% of 20 simulated 77-year histories "
         f"(seeds 600-619, never used in calibration); blue dot: their median. Black diamond: the real "
         f"S&P 500. Orange X: the original paper settings. The S&P falls inside the model's typical "
         f"range on {n_typ} of 10 measures; the paper settings miss volatility memory badly.")
    return pct


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 2
def fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
    pooled = np.concatenate([(r - r.mean()) / r.std() for r in cal_runs])
    for r, lab, c, ls in [(spx, "S&P 500 (real)", INK, "-"), (pooled, "calibrated model (20 histories)", BLUE, "-"),
                          (base, "no chartists (bell-curve news only)", AQUA, "-")]:
        z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
        ax.loglog(z, cc, ls, color=c, label=lab)
        ax.annotate(lab.split(" (")[0], (z[-1], cc[-1]), xytext=(5, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                    fontsize=8.5, color=INK, va="center")
    g = np.linspace(1, 9, 100)
    ax.loglog(g, 2 * norm.sf(g), "--", color=MUTED, lw=1.5, label="Gaussian (bell curve)")
    ax.loglog(g, 0.6 * g ** -3.0, ":", color=MUTED, lw=1.8, label="slope −3: inverse cubic law")
    ax.set_xlim(0.8, 40); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("size of daily move, in standard deviations (log scale)")
    ax.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("Fig 2. Fat tails: big days are far more common than a bell curve predicts")
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8.5)
    i = np.argmin(spx)
    ax.annotate("Black Monday 1987\n(23 std)", (abs(spx[i]) / spx.std(), 1 / len(spx)),
                xytext=(-110, 25), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8.5, color=INK,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED))
    save(fig, "fig2_tails.png",
         "On log-log axes a power law is a straight line. The real S&P and the calibrated model both "
         "follow the slope −3 line (the inverse cubic law, Gopikrishnan et al. 1998) over two orders of "
         "magnitude. With no chartists, the model's tail bends down exactly like the Gaussian: herding "
         "is what creates the fat tail.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 3
def fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
    lags = np.arange(1, 101)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[2, 1]))
    for ax, lg, f, title in [(axes[0], lags, np.abs, "Volatility memory: does a big move predict big moves later?"),
                             (axes[1], lags[:10], lambda x: x, "Return correlation: does today's direction predict tomorrow's?")]:
        cal = np.array([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in cal_runs])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(cal, [5, 50, 95], axis=0)
        ax.fill_between(lg, lo, hi, color=BLUE_LIGHT, alpha=0.6, lw=0, label="calibrated model, 5-95%")
        ax.plot(lg, med, color=BLUE, label="calibrated model, median")
        ax.plot(lg, np.median([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in paper_runs], axis=0), color=ORANGE,
                label="paper settings, median")
        ax.plot(lg, stats.acf(f(spx), lg), color=INK, label="S&P 500 (real)")
        ax.axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
        ax.set_xlabel("days apart (lag)"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("correlation")
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 3. Volatility clustering: the calibrated model remembers wild periods as long as the market does",
                 y=1.03, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig3_memory.png",
         "Left: correlation between the SIZE of moves k days apart. The S&P still remembers a wild "
         "period after 100 days; the paper settings forget within ~30 days; the calibrated model tracks "
         "the S&P. Right: correlation of DIRECTION. The real market is unpredictable (≈0). The model "
         "has a small 2-day reversal (the S&P is outside its typical range here: its known weak spot).")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 4
def fig_mechanism(p):
    o = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=604)
    r, frac, mis = o["r"][BURN:], o["frac"][BURN:], (o["lp"] - o["lf"])[BURN + 1:]
    i = int(np.argmin(r))
    w = slice(max(0, i - 400), min(len(r), i + 300))
    d = np.arange(len(r))[w] - i
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
    axes[0].plot(d, r[w] / r.std(), color=INK, lw=0.8)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("daily return\n(std units)")
    axes[0].set_title("① Returns: calm, then a burst of huge moves (the crash)", loc="left")
    axes[1].fill_between(d, 0, frac[w] * 100, color=BLUE, alpha=0.8, lw=0)
    axes[1].set_ylabel("chartists\n(% of traders)")
    axes[1].set_title("② Chartist share: traders crowd into trend-following, recruiting each other", loc="left")
    axes[2].plot(d, mis[w] * 100, color=ORANGE)
    axes[2].axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
    axes[2].set_ylabel("price vs value\n(% mispricing)")
    axes[2].set_title("③ Mispricing: with few fundamentalists left, nothing anchors the price", loc="left")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("days relative to the worst day of this history")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.axvline(0, color=RED, lw=1, ls="--")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 4. How the calibrated model makes a crash (a typical held-out history, seed 604)",
                 y=1.0, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig4_mechanism.png",
         "The same days in three panels. The crash (red line) comes when the share of chartists surges: "
         "each chartist makes it easier to recruit more (Kirman-style crowding), so fundamentalists "
         "dwindle and the price swings far from its value. As mispricing grows, betting on the price "
         "returning looks profitable, traders switch back to fundamentalist, and calm returns.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 5
def fig_kirman():
    cases = [("herding: ε < (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.002, delta=0.01)),
             ("no herding: ε > (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.05, delta=0.01))]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7))
    for col, (name, kw) in enumerate(cases):
        k = kirman.simulate(**kw, steps=40_000_000, seed=1)
        axes[0, col].plot(np.arange(0, len(k), 20_000) / 1e6, k[::20_000], color=BLUE, lw=1)
        axes[0, col].set_ylim(0, 100); axes[0, col].set_ylabel("ants at source A")
        axes[0, col].set_xlabel("steps (millions)"); axes[0, col].set_title(name)
        hist = np.bincount(k, minlength=101) / len(k)
        axes[1, col].bar(np.arange(101), hist, width=0.9, color=BLUE_LIGHT, label="simulation (40M steps)")
        axes[1, col].plot(np.arange(101), kirman.stationary(**kw), color=INK, lw=1.8,
                          label="Kirman's exact answer")
        tv = 0.5 * np.abs(hist - kirman.stationary(**kw)).sum()
        axes[1, col].set_xlabel("ants at source A"); axes[1, col].set_ylabel("share of time")
        axes[1, col].text(0.5, 0.92, f"mismatch (total variation) = {tv:.3f}", transform=axes[1, col].transAxes,
                          ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
        axes[1, col].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="center right" if col == 0 else "upper left")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 5. Kirman's ant model reproduces his exact math: herding makes the crowd flip all at once",
                 y=1.01, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig5_kirman.png",
         "100 ants choose between two identical food sources (N=100, δ=0.01). Left: when spontaneous "
         "switching ε is rarer than recruitment, ants herd at one source and then flip en masse. Right: "
         "otherwise they split about 50/50. Bottom: time spent at each state (bars) matches the exact "
         "long-run answer from detailed balance (line). This is the herding mechanism inside Lux-Marchesi.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 6
def fig_out_of_sample(pool, p):
    rows, names = [], []
    series = [("S&P 500 1950- (held-out seeds)", market_data.returns("spx").values),
              ("S&P 500 1928- (Great Depression)", market_data.returns("spx_1928").values),
              ("Nasdaq-100 1985-", market_data.returns("ndx").values)]
    series += [(f"stock {t}", market_data.stock_returns(t).values) for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
    cache = {}
    for name, r in series:
        n = len(r) if not name.startswith("stock") else 6700
        if n not in cache:
            cache[n] = [stats.stylized_facts(x) for x in ensemble(pool, p, range(700, 720), n)]
        pct = calibrate.percentiles(stats.stylized_facts(r), cache[n], calibrate.TARGETS)
        rows.append([pct[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS]); names.append(name)
    m = np.array(rows)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 10))
    from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
    cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", ["#256abf", "#9ec5f4", "#f0efec", "#f2a3a2", "#c53a39"])
    im = ax.imshow(m, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(m):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                color=INK, fontweight="bold" if not 5 <= v <= 95 else "normal")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(calibrate.TARGETS)), [LABELS[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS],
                  rotation=35, ha="right", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names, fontsize=8.5); ax.grid(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.6)
    cb.set_label("percentile of real data among 20 model histories\n(50 = perfectly typical; <5 or >95 = unusual)")
    ax.set_title("Fig 6. Out-of-sample: data the calibration never saw, scored against the model")
    unusual = int(np.sum((m < 5) | (m > 95)))
    save(fig, "fig6_out_of_sample.png",
         f"Gray cells are typical; strong blue/red cells (bold numbers) are unusual. With 10 measures and a "
         f"5-95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by chance alone. {unusual} of {m.size} "
         f"cells are unusual. The Nasdaq-100 and the 1928-2026 S&P (including the Great Depression) look "
         f"typical; stocks show more >4-std days than the model, because single companies also get "
         f"company-specific news (earnings surprises) that a whole-market model does not have.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 7
def _breaker_pair(args):
    p, seed, levels = args
    out = []
    for b in (None, dict(levels=levels, halt_minutes=15)):
        r = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=seed, breakers=b)["r"][BURN:]
        c = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(r)])
        out.append([-(c[k:] - c[:-k]).min() for k in (1, 5, 20)])
    return out


def fig_breakers(pool, p, cal_runs, spx):
    scale = np.median([r.std() for r in cal_runs]) / spx.std()
    levels = tuple(x * scale for x in (0.07, 0.13, 0.20))
    res = np.array(pool.map(_breaker_pair, [(p, s, levels) for s in range(3000, 3020)]))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.8))
    for j, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, ["worst single day", "worst 5-day fall", "worst 20-day fall"])):
        off, on = np.expm1(-res[:, 0, j]) * -100, np.expm1(-res[:, 1, j]) * -100
        top = max(off.max(), on.max()) * 1.08
        ax.plot([0, top], [0, top], color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
        ax.scatter(off, on, s=60, color=BLUE, edgecolor="#fcfcfb", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
        lower, higher = int(np.sum(on < off - 1e-9)), int(np.sum(on > off + 1e-9))
        ax.set_title(f"{name}\nlower with breakers in {lower}/20, higher in {higher}/20", fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel("fall without breakers (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("fall with breakers (%)")
        ax.set_xlim(0, top); ax.set_ylim(0, top)
        ax.text(0.05 * top, 0.9 * top, "below the line =\nbreakers helped", fontsize=8, color=SECOND)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 7. Circuit breakers soften the worst day but barely change multi-day crashes",
                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig7_circuit_breakers.png",
         f"Each dot is one 77-year history run twice with identical randomness: without and with US-style "
         f"circuit breakers (15-min pauses at −7% and −13%, close at −20%, scaled ×{scale:.2f} to the "
         f"model's volatility). Dots on the dashed line: no breaker ever fired. Breakers cut the worst "
         f"single day (~10%), but the 5- and 20-day falls barely move: pauses spread a crash over more "
         f"days rather than prevent it. This matches SEC findings on 1997 (halts did not clearly stabilize prices).")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 8
def _shock_pair(args):
    p, seed = args
    a = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed)
    b = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed, shocks={1000: -0.10})
    return a["frac"][999], (b["lp"] - a["lp"])[1000:1061]


def fig_shocks(pool, p):
    res = pool.map(_shock_pair, [(p, s) for s in range(5000, 5200)])
    frac = np.array([x[0] for x in res]); paths = np.array([x[1] for x in res])
    resp = paths / np.log(0.9)                       # 1.0 = moved exactly by the shock
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))
    for lo, hi, c, lab in [(0, 0.1, AQUA, "calm market (<10% chartists)"),
                           (0.3, 1.01, ORANGE, "crowded market (>30% chartists)")]:
        sel = (frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)
        axes[0].plot(np.arange(61), np.median(resp[sel], axis=0), color=c, label=f"{lab}, n={sel.sum()}")
        axes[0].fill_between(np.arange(61), np.percentile(resp[sel], 10, axis=0),
                             np.percentile(resp[sel], 90, axis=0), color=c, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    axes[0].axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("days after a surprise that cuts value 10%")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("price fall ÷ shock size\n(1.0 = moved exactly by the shock)")
    axes[0].set_title("Price response (median, 10-90% band)"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
    bins = [(0, 0.1), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 1.01)]
    over = [resp[(frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)].max(axis=1) for lo, hi in bins]
    names = ["<10%", "10-30%", ">30%"]
    axes[1].bar(names, [o.mean() for o in over], color=[AQUA, BLUE, ORANGE], width=0.55)
    for i, o in enumerate(over):
        axes[1].plot([i] * len(o), o, "o", color=INK, ms=3, alpha=0.35)
        axes[1].text(i, o.max() + 0.01, f"mean {o.mean():.2f}×\nmax {o.max():.2f}×", ha="center", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[1].set_ylim(0.95, max(o.max() for o in over) + 0.08)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("chartist share when the shock hits")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("largest fall ÷ shock size")
    axes[1].set_title("Overshoot depends on timing")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 8. A policy surprise is amplified only if it hits a market already full of trend-chasers",
                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig8_policy_shocks.png",
         "200 histories, each run twice with identical randomness: with and without a one-time surprise "
         "that cuts the fundamental value 10% (like an unexpected rate hike). In calm markets the price "
         "simply drops 10%. In crowded markets, chartists chase the fall and the price overshoots, by up "
         "to ~25%. In this model the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.")


def main():
    FIG.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    p = calibrate.load()
    spx = market_data.spx_returns().values
    with Pool() as pool:
        cal_runs = ensemble(pool, p)
        paper_runs = ensemble(pool, model.P)
        base = model.simulate(DAYS + BURN, False, p, seed=600)[0][BURN:]
        fig_fingerprint(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs)
        fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base)
        fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs)
        fig_mechanism(p)
        fig_kirman()
        fig_out_of_sample(pool, p)
        fig_breakers(pool, p, cal_runs, spx)
        fig_shocks(pool, p)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Make every results figure (figures/fig*.png) for the project write-up.

Run:  python3 make_figures.py      (~1-2 min with numba)
All model checks use held-out seeds the calibration never saw.
Colors (validated colorblind-safe): S&P/real data = ink, calibrated = blue,
paper settings = orange, no chartists = aqua, references = muted gray dashes.
"""
from multiprocessing import Pool

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

from herding import calibrate, kirman, market_data, model, stats

FIG = market_data.ROOT / "figures"
INK, SECOND, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9"
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, RED = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#e34948"
BLUE_LIGHT = "#b7d3f6"
DAYS, BURN = 19300, 300
HELD_OUT = range(600, 620)                       # never used by the calibration
LABELS = dict(alpha_5pct="tail exponent α (5% tail)", alpha_1pct="tail exponent α (1% tail)",
              share_4sd="share of days beyond 4 std", ac_r_1="return correlation, 1 day",
              ac_r_2="return correlation, 2 days", ac_r_2to10="return correlation, days 2-10",
              ac_abs_1="volatility memory, 1 day", ac_abs_20="volatility memory, 20 days",
              ac_abs_50="volatility memory, 50 days", ac_abs_100="volatility memory, 100 days")

plt.rcParams.update({
    "font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 10, "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.titleweight": "bold", "axes.edgecolor": "#c3c2b7", "axes.labelcolor": SECOND,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
    "grid.linewidth": 0.6, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "legend.frameon": False,
    "lines.linewidth": 2, "savefig.dpi": 150, "savefig.bbox": "tight"})


def save(fig, name, caption):
    fig.text(0.01, -0.02, caption, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=SECOND, wrap=True)
    fig.savefig(FIG / name)
    plt.close(fig)
    print("saved", name)


def _run(args):
    p, seed, days, herding = args
    return model.simulate(days + BURN, herding, p, seed=seed)[0][BURN:]


def ensemble(pool, p, seeds=HELD_OUT, days=DAYS, herding=True):
    return pool.map(_run, [(p, s, days, herding) for s in seeds])


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 1
def fig_fingerprint(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
    target = stats.stylized_facts(spx)
    cal = [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in cal_runs]
    paper = [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in paper_runs]
    pct = calibrate.percentiles(target, cal, calibrate.TARGETS)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(15, 5.6))
    for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, calibrate.TARGETS):
        v = np.array([f[k] for f in cal])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95])
        ax.plot([0, 0], [lo, hi], color=BLUE, lw=6, solid_capstyle="round", alpha=0.35)
        ax.plot(0, med, "o", color=BLUE, ms=8, label="calibrated model (median, 5-95%)")
        ax.plot(0.25, np.median([f[k] for f in paper]), "X", color=ORANGE, ms=9,
                label="paper settings (median)")
        ax.plot(-0.25, target[k], "D", color=INK, ms=8, label="S&P 500 1950-2026")
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 0.6); ax.set_xticks([])
        ax.set_title(LABELS[k], fontsize=9.5)
        flag = "typical" if 5 <= pct[k] <= 95 else "UNUSUAL"
        ax.text(0.5, 0.02, f"S&P percentile {pct[k]:.0f}% ({flag})", transform=ax.transAxes,
                ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK if flag == "typical" else RED)
    h, l = axes.flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(h, l, loc="upper center", ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.04))
    fig.suptitle("Fig 1. The S&P 500's fingerprint vs 20 held-out histories of the calibrated model",
                 y=1.10, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    n_typ = sum(5 <= v <= 95 for v in pct.values())
    save(fig, "fig1_fingerprint.png",
         f"Each panel is one measure. Blue bar: the range covering 90% of 20 simulated 77-year histories "
         f"(seeds 600-619, never used in calibration); blue dot: their median. Black diamond: the real "
         f"S&P 500. Orange X: the original paper settings. The S&P falls inside the model's typical "
         f"range on {n_typ} of 10 measures; the paper settings miss volatility memory badly.")
    return pct


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 2
def fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
    pooled = np.concatenate([(r - r.mean()) / r.std() for r in cal_runs])
    for r, lab, c, ls in [(spx, "S&P 500 (real)", INK, "-"), (pooled, "calibrated model (20 histories)", BLUE, "-"),
                          (base, "no chartists (bell-curve news only)", AQUA, "-")]:
        z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
        ax.loglog(z, cc, ls, color=c, label=lab)
        ax.annotate(lab.split(" (")[0], (z[-1], cc[-1]), xytext=(5, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                    fontsize=8.5, color=INK, va="center")
    g = np.linspace(1, 9, 100)
    ax.loglog(g, 2 * norm.sf(g), "--", color=MUTED, lw=1.5, label="Gaussian (bell curve)")
    ax.loglog(g, 0.6 * g ** -3.0, ":", color=MUTED, lw=1.8, label="slope −3: inverse cubic law")
    ax.set_xlim(0.8, 40); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("size of daily move, in standard deviations (log scale)")
    ax.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("Fig 2. Fat tails: big days are far more common than a bell curve predicts")
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8.5)
    i = np.argmin(spx)
    ax.annotate("Black Monday 1987\n(23 std)", (abs(spx[i]) / spx.std(), 1 / len(spx)),
                xytext=(-110, 25), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8.5, color=INK,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED))
    save(fig, "fig2_tails.png",
         "On log-log axes a power law is a straight line. The real S&P and the calibrated model both "
         "follow the slope −3 line (the inverse cubic law, Gopikrishnan et al. 1998) over two orders of "
         "magnitude. With no chartists, the model's tail bends down exactly like the Gaussian: herding "
         "is what creates the fat tail.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 3
def fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
    lags = np.arange(1, 101)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[2, 1]))
    for ax, lg, f, title in [(axes[0], lags, np.abs, "Volatility memory: does a big move predict big moves later?"),
                             (axes[1], lags[:10], lambda x: x, "Return correlation: does today's direction predict tomorrow's?")]:
        cal = np.array([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in cal_runs])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(cal, [5, 50, 95], axis=0)
        ax.fill_between(lg, lo, hi, color=BLUE_LIGHT, alpha=0.6, lw=0, label="calibrated model, 5-95%")
        ax.plot(lg, med, color=BLUE, label="calibrated model, median")
        ax.plot(lg, np.median([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in paper_runs], axis=0), color=ORANGE,
                label="paper settings, median")
        ax.plot(lg, stats.acf(f(spx), lg), color=INK, label="S&P 500 (real)")
        ax.axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
        ax.set_xlabel("days apart (lag)"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("correlation")
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 3. Volatility clustering: the calibrated model remembers wild periods as long as the market does",
                 y=1.03, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig3_memory.png",
         "Left: correlation between the SIZE of moves k days apart. The S&P still remembers a wild "
         "period after 100 days; the paper settings forget within ~30 days; the calibrated model tracks "
         "the S&P. Right: correlation of DIRECTION. The real market is unpredictable (≈0). The model "
         "has a small 2-day reversal (the S&P is outside its typical range here: its known weak spot).")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 4
def fig_mechanism(p):
    o = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=604)
    r, frac, mis = o["r"][BURN:], o["frac"][BURN:], (o["lp"] - o["lf"])[BURN + 1:]
    i = int(np.argmin(r))
    w = slice(max(0, i - 400), min(len(r), i + 300))
    d = np.arange(len(r))[w] - i
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
    axes[0].plot(d, r[w] / r.std(), color=INK, lw=0.8)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("daily return\n(std units)")
    axes[0].set_title("① Returns: calm, then a burst of huge moves (the crash)", loc="left")
    axes[1].fill_between(d, 0, frac[w] * 100, color=BLUE, alpha=0.8, lw=0)
    axes[1].set_ylabel("chartists\n(% of traders)")
    axes[1].set_title("② Chartist share: traders crowd into trend-following, recruiting each other", loc="left")
    axes[2].plot(d, mis[w] * 100, color=ORANGE)
    axes[2].axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
    axes[2].set_ylabel("price vs value\n(% mispricing)")
    axes[2].set_title("③ Mispricing: with few fundamentalists left, nothing anchors the price", loc="left")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("days relative to the worst day of this history")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.axvline(0, color=RED, lw=1, ls="--")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 4. How the calibrated model makes a crash (a typical held-out history, seed 604)",
                 y=1.0, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig4_mechanism.png",
         "The same days in three panels. The crash (red line) comes when the share of chartists surges: "
         "each chartist makes it easier to recruit more (Kirman-style crowding), so fundamentalists "
         "dwindle and the price swings far from its value. As mispricing grows, betting on the price "
         "returning looks profitable, traders switch back to fundamentalist, and calm returns.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 5
def fig_kirman():
    cases = [("herding: ε < (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.002, delta=0.01)),
             ("no herding: ε > (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.05, delta=0.01))]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7))
    for col, (name, kw) in enumerate(cases):
        k = kirman.simulate(**kw, steps=40_000_000, seed=1)
        axes[0, col].plot(np.arange(0, len(k), 20_000) / 1e6, k[::20_000], color=BLUE, lw=1)
        axes[0, col].set_ylim(0, 100); axes[0, col].set_ylabel("ants at source A")
        axes[0, col].set_xlabel("steps (millions)"); axes[0, col].set_title(name)
        hist = np.bincount(k, minlength=101) / len(k)
        axes[1, col].bar(np.arange(101), hist, width=0.9, color=BLUE_LIGHT, label="simulation (40M steps)")
        axes[1, col].plot(np.arange(101), kirman.stationary(**kw), color=INK, lw=1.8,
                          label="Kirman's exact answer")
        tv = 0.5 * np.abs(hist - kirman.stationary(**kw)).sum()
        axes[1, col].set_xlabel("ants at source A"); axes[1, col].set_ylabel("share of time")
        axes[1, col].text(0.5, 0.92, f"mismatch (total variation) = {tv:.3f}", transform=axes[1, col].transAxes,
                          ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
        axes[1, col].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="center right" if col == 0 else "upper left")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 5. Kirman's ant model reproduces his exact math: herding makes the crowd flip all at once",
                 y=1.01, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig5_kirman.png",
         "100 ants choose between two identical food sources (N=100, δ=0.01). Left: when spontaneous "
         "switching ε is rarer than recruitment, ants herd at one source and then flip en masse. Right: "
         "otherwise they split about 50/50. Bottom: time spent at each state (bars) matches the exact "
         "long-run answer from detailed balance (line). This is the herding mechanism inside Lux-Marchesi.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 6
def fig_out_of_sample(pool, p):
    rows, names = [], []
    series = [("S&P 500 1950- (held-out seeds)", market_data.returns("spx").values),
              ("S&P 500 1928- (Great Depression)", market_data.returns("spx_1928").values),
              ("Nasdaq-100 1985-", market_data.returns("ndx").values)]
    series += [(f"stock {t}", market_data.stock_returns(t).values) for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
    cache = {}
    for name, r in series:
        n = len(r) if not name.startswith("stock") else 6700
        if n not in cache:
            cache[n] = [stats.stylized_facts(x) for x in ensemble(pool, p, range(700, 720), n)]
        pct = calibrate.percentiles(stats.stylized_facts(r), cache[n], calibrate.TARGETS)
        rows.append([pct[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS]); names.append(name)
    m = np.array(rows)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 10))
    from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
    cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", ["#256abf", "#9ec5f4", "#f0efec", "#f2a3a2", "#c53a39"])
    im = ax.imshow(m, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(m):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                color=INK, fontweight="bold" if not 5 <= v <= 95 else "normal")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(calibrate.TARGETS)), [LABELS[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS],
                  rotation=35, ha="right", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names, fontsize=8.5); ax.grid(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.6)
    cb.set_label("percentile of real data among 20 model histories\n(50 = perfectly typical; <5 or >95 = unusual)")
    ax.set_title("Fig 6. Out-of-sample: data the calibration never saw, scored against the model")
    unusual = int(np.sum((m < 5) | (m > 95)))
    save(fig, "fig6_out_of_sample.png",
         f"Gray cells are typical; strong blue/red cells (bold numbers) are unusual. With 10 measures and a "
         f"5-95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by chance alone. {unusual} of {m.size} "
         f"cells are unusual. The Nasdaq-100 and the 1928-2026 S&P (including the Great Depression) look "
         f"typical; stocks show more >4-std days than the model, because single companies also get "
         f"company-specific news (earnings surprises) that a whole-market model does not have.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 7
def _breaker_pair(args):
    p, seed, levels = args
    out = []
    for b in (None, dict(levels=levels, halt_minutes=15)):
        r = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=seed, breakers=b)["r"][BURN:]
        c = np.concatenate([[0.0], np.cumsum(r)])
        out.append([-(c[k:] - c[:-k]).min() for k in (1, 5, 20)])
    return out


def fig_breakers(pool, p, cal_runs, spx):
    scale = np.median([r.std() for r in cal_runs]) / spx.std()
    levels = tuple(x * scale for x in (0.07, 0.13, 0.20))
    res = np.array(pool.map(_breaker_pair, [(p, s, levels) for s in range(3000, 3020)]))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.8))
    for j, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, ["worst single day", "worst 5-day fall", "worst 20-day fall"])):
        off, on = np.expm1(-res[:, 0, j]) * -100, np.expm1(-res[:, 1, j]) * -100
        top = max(off.max(), on.max()) * 1.08
        ax.plot([0, top], [0, top], color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
        ax.scatter(off, on, s=60, color=BLUE, edgecolor="#fcfcfb", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
        lower, higher = int(np.sum(on < off - 1e-9)), int(np.sum(on > off + 1e-9))
        ax.set_title(f"{name}\nlower with breakers in {lower}/20, higher in {higher}/20", fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel("fall without breakers (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("fall with breakers (%)")
        ax.set_xlim(0, top); ax.set_ylim(0, top)
        ax.text(0.05 * top, 0.9 * top, "below the line =\nbreakers helped", fontsize=8, color=SECOND)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 7. Circuit breakers soften the worst day but barely change multi-day crashes",
                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig7_circuit_breakers.png",
         f"Each dot is one 77-year history run twice with identical randomness: without and with US-style "
         f"circuit breakers (15-min pauses at −7% and −13%, close at −20%, scaled ×{scale:.2f} to the "
         f"model's volatility). Dots on the dashed line: no breaker ever fired. Breakers cut the worst "
         f"single day (~10%), but the 5- and 20-day falls barely move: pauses spread a crash over more "
         f"days rather than prevent it. This matches SEC findings on 1997 (halts did not clearly stabilize prices).")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 8
def _shock_pair(args):
    p, seed = args
    a = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed)
    b = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed, shocks={1000: -0.10})
    return a["frac"][999], (b["lp"] - a["lp"])[1000:1061]


def fig_shocks(pool, p):
    res = pool.map(_shock_pair, [(p, s) for s in range(5000, 5200)])
    frac = np.array([x[0] for x in res]); paths = np.array([x[1] for x in res])
    resp = paths / np.log(0.9)                       # 1.0 = moved exactly by the shock
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))
    for lo, hi, c, lab in [(0, 0.1, AQUA, "calm market (<10% chartists)"),
                           (0.3, 1.01, ORANGE, "crowded market (>30% chartists)")]:
        sel = (frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)
        axes[0].plot(np.arange(61), np.median(resp[sel], axis=0), color=c, label=f"{lab}, n={sel.sum()}")
        axes[0].fill_between(np.arange(61), np.percentile(resp[sel], 10, axis=0),
                             np.percentile(resp[sel], 90, axis=0), color=c, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    axes[0].axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("days after a surprise that cuts value 10%")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("price fall ÷ shock size\n(1.0 = moved exactly by the shock)")
    axes[0].set_title("Price response (median, 10-90% band)"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
    bins = [(0, 0.1), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 1.01)]
    over = [resp[(frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)].max(axis=1) for lo, hi in bins]
    names = ["<10%", "10-30%", ">30%"]
    axes[1].bar(names, [o.mean() for o in over], color=[AQUA, BLUE, ORANGE], width=0.55)
    for i, o in enumerate(over):
        axes[1].plot([i] * len(o), o, "o", color=INK, ms=3, alpha=0.35)
        axes[1].text(i, o.max() + 0.01, f"mean {o.mean():.2f}×\nmax {o.max():.2f}×", ha="center", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[1].set_ylim(0.95, max(o.max() for o in over) + 0.08)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("chartist share when the shock hits")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("largest fall ÷ shock size")
    axes[1].set_title("Overshoot depends on timing")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 8. A policy surprise is amplified only if it hits a market already full of trend-chasers",
                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig8_policy_shocks.png",
         "200 histories, each run twice with identical randomness: with and without a one-time surprise "
         "that cuts the fundamental value 10% (like an unexpected rate hike). In calm markets the price "
         "simply drops 10%. In crowded markets, chartists chase the fall and the price overshoots, by up "
         "to ~25%. In this model the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.")


def main():
    FIG.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    p = calibrate.load()
    spx = market_data.spx_returns().values
    with Pool() as pool:
        cal_runs = ensemble(pool, p)
        paper_runs = ensemble(pool, model.P)
        base = model.simulate(DAYS + BURN, False, p, seed=600)[0][BURN:]
        fig_fingerprint(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs)
        fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base)
        fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs)
        fig_mechanism(p)
        fig_kirman()
        fig_out_of_sample(pool, p)
        fig_breakers(pool, p, cal_runs, spx)
        fig_shocks(pool, p)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Results: Can herding explain market crashes?

All figures are made by `python3 make_figures.py` (about 1 minute). Every model check
uses **held-out seeds** that the calibration never saw, so the model is not graded on
its own homework. Colors mean the same thing in every figure:

| Color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Black | the real market (S&P 500 or other real data) |
| Blue | the **calibrated** Lux–Marchesi model (settings fitted to the S&P 500) |
| Orange | the model with the **original 1999 paper settings** |
| Aqua | the model with **no chartists** (bell-curve news only; the base case) |
| Gray dashes | reference lines (bell curve, slope −3) |

**Key vocabulary**
- **Fundamentalist:** a trader who buys when the price is below the company's true value and sells when it's above.
- **Chartist:** a trader who ignores value and follows the trend and the crowd.
- **Fat tail:** big days happen far more often than a bell curve says.
- **Tail exponent α:** how fast big days become rare; smaller α means more crashes, and real markets have α ≈ 3.
- **Volatility clustering / memory:** big moves come in bunches, so a wild day predicts more wild days later.
- **Percentile:** where the real value falls among 20 simulated histories. 50% is perfectly typical; below 5% or above 95% is unusual.

---

## Fig 1. The S&P 500's fingerprint vs the calibrated model
![](fig1_fingerprint.png)

**Question:** does the real S&P 500 (1950–2026) look like a typical history of the model?

**How to read it:** each of the 10 panels is one measure of how a market behaves.
- The **blue bar** spans 90% of 20 simulated 77-year histories, and the blue dot is their median.
- The **black diamond** is the real S&P 500.
- The **orange X** is the paper's original settings.

**Result:**
- The real S&P sits inside the calibrated model's typical range on **9 of 10** measures.
- The one miss is the **2-day return correlation**: after a big move, the model tends to partly reverse it two days later more than the real market does. This is the model's known weak spot.
- The paper settings miss badly on volatility memory at 20, 50 and 100 days. They forget wild periods almost immediately.

## Fig 2. Fat tails
![](fig2_tails.png)

**Question:** are big days more common than a bell curve predicts, and does herding cause it?

**How to read it:** this is a log-log plot, which turns a power law into a straight line. The x-axis is the size of a daily move in standard deviations; the y-axis is the share of days with an even bigger move.

**Result:**
- The real S&P and the calibrated model both run along the **slope −3 line**, the inverse cubic law found by Gopikrishnan et al. (1998). Moves are 8 times rarer each time their size doubles.
- With **no chartists**, the model's tail drops away exactly like the bell curve.
- **This is the proposal's central check:** the news is a bell curve in both runs, so the fat tail comes from the traders, not the news.
- Black Monday 1987 (23 standard deviations) sits at the far right. The model produces days of 20+ standard deviations too.

## Fig 3. Volatility clustering and predictability
![](fig3_memory.png)

**Left, volatility memory:** does a big move today predict big moves k days later?
- The real S&P still "remembers" a wild period after 100 days (correlation about 0.09).
- The calibrated model's median follows the S&P almost exactly.
- The paper settings forget within about 30 days.

**Right, return correlation:** does today's *direction* predict tomorrow's?
- In the real market, no: it's about 0. If direction were predictable, traders would trade the pattern away.
- The model has a small reversal over days 2–5, the same weak spot as in Fig 1.

## Fig 4. How the calibrated model makes a crash
![](fig4_mechanism.png)

**How to read it:** the same 700 days of one typical held-out history, shown in three panels.

**Result, the crash cycle:**
1. A few traders become chartists, and each one makes it easier to recruit more. Their share snowballs from about 2% to nearly 100% (panel ②).
2. With almost no fundamentalists left, nothing pulls the price back toward its value. The price swings up to 30% away from it (panel ③), and returns explode to 20 standard deviations (panel ①).
3. Once the price is far from its value, betting on its return looks profitable. Traders drift back to being fundamentalists, and calm returns.

**This answers the project question:** in this model, crashes come from *herding into the trend-following strategy* (copying strategy), not from bad news.

## Fig 5. Kirman's ant model (the proposal's first check)
![](fig5_kirman.png)

**Setup:** 100 ants choose between two identical food sources. Each step, one ant either switches on its own (probability ε) or is recruited by another ant.

**Result:**
- When spontaneous switching is rarer than recruitment (left), the ants **herd**: most of them sit at one source, then the whole crowd flips.
- Otherwise (right), they split about 50/50.
- In the bottom panels, the time the simulation spends at each state (bars) matches **Kirman's exact formula** (line), with a mismatch of only 0.020 and 0.004.
- This is the recruitment mechanism that Lux–Marchesi uses for traders.

## Fig 6. Out-of-sample test: data the calibration never saw
![](fig6_out_of_sample.png)

**How to read it:** each row is a real data series and each column a measure. A cell is the real data's percentile among 20 model histories. Gray means typical; strong blue or red with a bold number means unusual. With 10 measures and a 5–95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by pure chance.

**Result:**
- Only 6 of 230 cells are unusual, fewer than chance alone would produce.
- The **Nasdaq-100** looks typical on every measure, and so does the **S&P 500 from 1928**, including the 1929 crash and the Great Depression, except one cell (the reversal again).
- The **20 stocks with market beta 0.9–1.1** (stocks that move about 1-for-1 with the market) mostly look typical. Some show more extreme days than the model. That's expected: single companies also get company-specific news (earnings surprises, lawsuits) that a whole-market model doesn't have.

**Caveat:** the stocks are companies that are large *today*, so failed firms are missing (survivorship bias).

## Fig 7. Policy experiment 1: circuit breakers
![](fig7_circuit_breakers.png)

**Setup:**
- Each dot is one 77-year history, run twice with **identical randomness**: once without and once with US-style circuit breakers. The real rules since 2013 are 15-minute pauses at −7% and −13% and a full-day close at −20%; here they're scaled ×1.34 to match the model's volatility.
- Dots below the dashed line mean breakers helped.
- Dots exactly on the line are histories where no breaker ever fired.

**Result:**
- Breakers lower the **worst single day** in 14 of 20 histories, by about 10%.
- But the **worst 5-day and 20-day falls** barely change: only 11 of 20 histories improve over 20 days, close to a coin flip.
- Pauses **spread a crash over more days rather than prevent it**, because they don't change why traders crowd into trend-following.
- This agrees with the SEC staff's finding that the 1997 halts did not clearly stabilize prices.

## Fig 8. Policy experiment 2: a policy surprise (like an unexpected rate hike)
![](fig8_policy_shocks.png)

**Setup:**
- 200 histories, each run twice with identical randomness: with and without a one-time surprise that cuts the company's true value by 10%.
- The surprise stands in for real events such as an unexpected Fed rate hike, the 1930 tariffs, or the 2011 US credit downgrade.

**Result:**
- In a **calm market** (under 10% chartists), the price simply falls 10%, exactly the size of the surprise.
- In a **crowded market** (over 30% chartists), trend-chasers pile on and the fall **overshoots by up to about 25%**: a 10% surprise becomes about a 12.5% fall.
- **In this model, the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.** The same news is harmless in a calm market and amplified in a crowded one.

---

## Honest limitations
1. **Two-day reversal.** After a big move the model slightly reverses it over the next 2–5 days, and the real market does not (Figs 1, 3, 6).
2. **One market, no individual companies.** The model can't produce company-specific shocks or insider trading.
3. **Changes from the 1999 paper.** Log prices, a faster market maker, and minimum group sizes were needed to fix bugs, so the model is not the paper's exact equations.
4. **Large differences between histories.** Even with the same settings, one 77-year history can be calm and another full of crashes. A single history (including the real one) is weak evidence on its own; that's why every check here uses 20.
5. **Policy experiments are stylized.** Breaker timing rules are simplified (no 3:25 pm cutoff), and a "policy surprise" is a one-time jump in value, not a model of the Fed.

- In the bottom panels, the time the simulation spends at each state (bars) matches **Kirman's exact formula** (line), with a mismatch of only 0.020 and 0.004.
- This is the recruitment mechanism that Lux–Marchesi uses for traders.

## Fig 6. Out-of-sample test: data the calibration never saw
![](fig6_out_of_sample.png)

**How to read it:** each row is a real data series and each column a measure. A cell is the real data's percentile among 20 model histories. Gray means typical; strong blue or red with a bold number means unusual. With 10 measures and a 5–95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by pure chance.

**Result:**
- Only 6 of 230 cells are unusual, fewer than chance alone would produce.
- The **Nasdaq-100** looks typical on every measure, and so does the **S&P 500 from 1928**, including the 1929 crash and the Great Depression, except one cell (the reversal again).
- The **20 stocks with market beta 0.9–1.1** (stocks that move about 1-for-1 with the market) mostly look typical. Some show more extreme days than the model. That's expected: single companies also get company-specific news (earnings surprises, lawsuits) that a whole-market model doesn't have.

**Caveat:** the stocks are companies that are large *today*, so failed firms are missing (survivorship bias).

## Fig 7. Policy experiment 1: circuit breakers
![](fig7_circuit_breakers.png)

**Setup:**
- Each dot is one 77-year history, run twice with **identical randomness**: once without and once with US-style circuit breakers. The real rules since 2013 are 15-minute pauses at −7% and −13% and a full-day close at −20%; here they're scaled ×1.34 to match the model's volatility.
- Dots below the dashed line mean breakers helped.
- Dots exactly on the line are histories where no breaker ever fired.

**Result:**
- Breakers lower the **worst single day** in 14 of 20 histories, by about 10%.
- But the **worst 5-day and 20-day falls** barely change: only 11 of 20 histories improve over 20 days, close to a coin flip.
- Pauses **spread a crash over more days rather than prevent it**, because they don't change why traders crowd into trend-following.
- This agrees with the SEC staff's finding that the 1997 halts did not clearly stabilize prices.

## Fig 8. Policy experiment 2: a policy surprise (like an unexpected rate hike)
![](fig8_policy_shocks.png)

**Setup:**
- 200 histories, each run twice with identical randomness: with and without a one-time surprise that cuts the company's true value by 10%.
- The surprise stands in for real events such as an unexpected Fed rate hike, the 1930 tariffs, or the 2011 US credit downgrade.

**Result:**
- In a **calm market** (under 10% chartists), the price simply falls 10%, exactly the size of the surprise.
- In a **crowded market** (over 30% chartists), trend-chasers pile on and the fall **overshoots by up to about 25%**: a 10% surprise becomes about a 12.5% fall.
- **In this model, the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.** The same news is harmless in a calm market and amplified in a crowded one.

---

## Honest limitations
1. **Two-day reversal.** After a big move the model slightly reverses it over the next 2–5 days, and the real market does not (Figs 1, 3, 6).
2. **One market, no individual companies.** The model can't produce company-specific shocks or insider trading.
3. **Changes from the 1999 paper.** Log prices, a faster market maker, and minimum group sizes were needed to fix bugs, so the model is not the paper's exact equations.
4. **Large differences between histories.** Even with the same settings, one 77-year history can be calm and another full of crashes. A single history (including the real one) is weak evidence on its own; that's why every check here uses 20.
5. **Policy experiments are stylized.** Breaker timing rules are simplified (no 3:25 pm cutoff), and a "policy surprise" is a one-time jump in value, not a model of the Fed.

"""Can herding explain market crashes? Lux-Marchesi model vs the S&P 500.

Run:  python3 main.py   -> prints the comparison, saves figures/draft.png
Test: python3 -m pytest tests/ -q          (quick: add  -m "not slow")
"""
import numpy as np

from herding import calibrate, model, plots, stats
from herding import market_data as data

FIGURES = data.ROOT / "figures"
DAYS, BURN = 19300, 300         # same length as the S&P 500 sample; drop start-up transient
HISTORIES = 20                  # the model has randomness: judge it over many histories
SEEDS = range(600, 600 + HISTORIES)   # held out: never used by the calibration


def run_model(p=model.P, herding=True, seed=1, days=DAYS):
    r, frac = model.simulate(days + BURN, herding=herding, p=p, seed=seed)
    return r[BURN:], frac[BURN:]


def compare(series):
    """Table of stylized facts, one column per named return series."""
    facts = {name: stats.stylized_facts(r) for name, r in series.items()}
    rows = list(next(iter(facts.values())))
    lines = [f"{'':<12}" + "".join(f"{n:>16}" for n in facts)]
    for k in rows:
        lines.append(f"{k:<12}" + "".join(f"{facts[n][k]:>16.3f}" for n in facts))
    return "\n".join(lines)


def ensemble(p, seeds, days=DAYS):
    """Returns and stylized facts of several simulated histories."""
    runs = [run_model(p, seed=s, days=days) for s in seeds]
    return runs, [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r, _ in runs]


def ensemble_table(target, cal, paper):
    """S&P value, calibrated median [5-95% range], S&P percentile, paper median."""
    pct = calibrate.percentiles(target, cal, target)
    lines = [f"{'fact':<12}{'S&P 500':>9}{'calibrated (5-95% range)':>30}"
             f"{'S&P pct':>9}{'paper set':>11}"]
    for k in target:
        v = np.array([f[k] for f in cal])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95])
        flag = "" if 5 <= pct[k] <= 95 else " <- unusual"
        lines.append(f"{k:<12}{target[k]:>9.3f}{med:>12.3f} ({lo:7.3f} to {hi:7.3f})"
                     f"{pct[k]:>8.0f}%{np.median([f[k] for f in paper]):>11.3f}{flag}")
    return "\n".join(lines)


def main(p=None, out=FIGURES / "draft.png", histories=HISTORIES, days=DAYS):
    """Compare the S&P 500 with many histories of the calibrated model and the
    paper's original settings, plus the no-chartist base case; save a figure
    of the most typical calibrated history (median mismatch, not the best)."""
    p = calibrate.load() if p is None else p
    real = data.spx_returns()
    bm = data.black_monday(real)
    real = real.values
    print(f"S&P 500: {len(real)} daily returns")
    print(f"Black Monday 1987: {np.expm1(bm):.1%} (log return {bm:.3f}) = "
          f"{abs(bm) / real.std():.1f} standard deviations")
    seeds = SEEDS[:histories]
    runs, cal = ensemble(p, seeds, days)
    _, paper = ensemble(model.P, seeds, days)
    target = stats.stylized_facts(real)
    print(f"\n{histories} simulated histories of {days} days each:")
    print(ensemble_table(target, cal, paper))
    i = calibrate.representative(cal, target)
    herd, frac = runs[i]
    base, _ = run_model(p, herding=False, seed=0, days=days)
    print(f"no-chartist base case: kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(base):.3f} (bell curve = 0)")
    plots.comparison(real, herd, frac, base, out)
    print(f"\nSaved {out} (typical history: seed {seeds[i]})")
    return real, herd, base


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

I condensed the code so that shared logic lives in one place, and nothing changed in what it produces. I checked each output against a saved copy from before the cleanup:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `main.py` printout | Identical |
| All 9 figures | Byte-for-byte identical files |
| Out-of-sample and circuit-breaker results | Identical |
| Calibration measurements | Identical |
| `model.py` and `calibrated_params.json` | Unchanged |
| Tests | 426 pass, plus the 2 known limitations |

**What changed:**
- **New `herding/experiments.py`.** The logic for running the model many times, dropping the start-up days, finding the worst multi-day fall, and scaling the circuit-breaker rules was written separately in 5 files. Now it's written once and used by `main.py`, `make_figures.py`, `calibrate.py`, `analysis/out_of_sample.py` and `analysis/circuit_breakers.py`. It has its own 8 tests, including hand-worked worst-fall cases.
- **`main.py` is faster: 13 seconds instead of 20,** because its 40 simulations now run in parallel.
- **Removed dead code:** `main.compare()` was never called.
- **`tests/experiments.py` moved to `analysis/stress_tests.py`.** It was an exploration script, not a test. It still produces the same figures.

**Left alone on purpose:**
- **The old probe scripts in `analysis/`.** They're the record behind each finding in your journal, so I didn't merge them.
- **Speeding up `stylized_facts`.** I measured it at 5 ms per call, so it wasn't worth the change.

Separately, the interest-rate files `data/fred_*.csv` are downloaded but not used by anything yet. They're for the policy-timeline step we haven't done.

There's a lot uncommitted now: the bug fixes, circuit breakers, policy shocks, new market data, figures, `RESULTS.md`, this cleanup and your notes. What commit message do you want?

# Can Herding Explain Market Crashes?

## Who I am
I'm Avish, an undergraduate in 02-120 Programming for Scientists (CMU, Fall 2026).
This repository is my final project. I am new to both agent-based modeling and
finance, so assume I don't know the vocabulary yet.

## How I like to learn
- Teach me one idea at a time, in plain language, and define each term before you use it.
- Quiz me with small exercises instead of asking "does that make sense?" (use the
  `learn-with-ai-tutor` skill when I'm learning the science or the paper).
- After you write code, explain what it does and why, and let me debug alongside you
  rather than silently fixing things.
- Prove that code is right, not just that it runs (use the `test-every-function` skill).

## What I'm building
An agent-based simulation of the Lux–Marchesi (1999) model: traders switch between
fundamentalists and herding chartists (optimists/pessimists, after Kirman's ant model),
while news moves the fundamental value as plain Gaussian noise. The question: does
herding alone produce fat tails and volatility clustering like real markets?
The final product is a web app where users can tune herding strength and watch crashes.

### Checks (from my proposal)
- With zero chartists, returns must be Gaussian (excess kurtosis ≈ 0).
- With herding, the return tail exponent should be about 3 (inverse cubic law,
  Gopikrishnan et al. 1998), and S&P 500 data should show this too.
- Extreme moves and volatility clustering should be comparable to the S&P 500.
- Later: reproduce Kirman's ant model first as a check against his math.

## Where things live
- `main.py`: runs the comparison (S&P 500 vs 20 calibrated histories vs paper settings), saves `figures/draft.png`
- `herding/`: the program, one module per job
  - `model.py`: the Lux-Marchesi simulation, guardrails, optional circuit breakers (numba-accelerated)
  - `stats.py`: tail exponent, kurtosis, autocorrelation, the "stylized facts" fingerprint
  - `market_data.py`: loads and checks `data/spx_daily.csv`
  - `kirman.py`: Kirman's ant model with its exact solution (the herding check from the proposal)
  - `calibrate.py`: fits settings to the S&P 500 (`python3 -m herding.calibrate`) -> `calibrated_params.json`
  - `plots.py`: figures (reusable by the future web app)
- `tests/`: one test file per module; `python3 -m pytest tests/ -q` (quick: add `-m "not slow"`);
  `tests/experiments.py` makes `figures/test_*.png`
- `analysis/`: exploration scripts behind each finding, plus `history/` (earlier versions)
- `data/`: S&P 500 daily closes 1950-today and 1928-today (Yahoo ^GSPC), Nasdaq-100 (^NDX, 1985-),
  `stocks/` (20 large stocks with market beta 0.9-1.1, 2000-), VIX, NBER recessions (FRED USREC)
- `paper/`: sources. The Lux & Marchesi Nature paper (doi:10.1038/17290) is paywalled
  and still needs to be added via CMU library access.
- `notes/`: my own notes from tutoring sessions
- `scratch/`: temporary files (git-ignored)
- `journal/`: build journal logs (copied automatically; don't edit by hand)

## Working rules
- Keep the smallest working version checked before adding features.
- Commit messages should be in my own words; ask me for one if I haven't given it.
- This repo is public: never put passwords, API keys, or personal info in it.

- [Keep files in project folder](keep-files-in-project-folder.md) — every file I create goes inside 02-120 Project (use scratch/), never the scratchpad or /tmp
- [Prompt suggestions off while tutoring](prompt-suggestions-off-while-tutoring.md) — turn prompt_suggestions off for tutoring, back on when tutoring ends

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   - **Project:** Avish (CMU 02-120 Programming for Scientists, Fall 2026) is building the final project "Can Herding Explain Market Crashes? Reproducing the Lux–Marchesi Model With Today's S&P 500 Data." It is an agent-based model with fundamentalists and herding chartists (Kirman ants), and the news is Gaussian. The checks are:
     - zero chartists gives Gaussian returns (kurtosis ≈ 0);
     - with herding, the tail exponent α ≈ 3 (inverse cubic law, Gopikrishnan 1998);
     - fat tails and volatility clustering comparable to the S&P;
     - reproduce Kirman's ant model first.
   - **Final product:** an interactive web app (the HTML webpage is not built yet).
   - **Requests so far, in order:**
     - quick draft main.py;
     - build journal setup per the course page;
     - GitHub repo, made public;
     - course claude-setup (CLAUDE.md plus skills);
     - VS Code plus the Claude extension;
     - tutoring sessions;
     - test every function;
     - fix all problems;
     - guardrails;
     - a 45–60 minute improvement push (calibrate first, model only, split modules, no commits);
     - split into modules, then the herding/ package plus plots.py;
     - teach the calibrated model;
     - more data (S&P since 1928, Nasdaq-100, stocks matched by market beta) and a circuit-breaker policy experiment;
     - research on US government/Fed/economic policy history and using it;
     - review decisions and bugs;
     - fix 4 bugs without affecting the model or calibration;
     - make annotated figures plus text;
     - condense code without changing functionality;
     - double-check everything with all tests;
     - commit and push.
   - **Most recent request:** "comit and push to repo". This is done.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Lux–Marchesi model:**
     - fundamentalists vs optimist/pessimist chartists;
     - switching rates are exponentials of U1/U21/U22;
     - Kirman-style recruitment;
     - a market maker driven by excess demand;
     - log prices, so the model is invariant to price level;
     - a smoothed trend (tau);
     - floors: min_chartists per type and min fundamentalists;
     - start at about 10% chartists.
   - **Measures and calibration:**
     - stylized-facts fingerprint: Hill α (5% and 1% tails), share of days beyond 4σ, return ACF (lag 1, lag 2, mean of lags 2–10), and |r| ACF at lags 1, 20, 50, 100; kurtosis is reported but not targeted;
     - calibration loss is the sum of squared gaps in SCALE units;
     - Latin hypercube search plus local refine;
     - held-out seeds and percentile "typicality" across 20 histories; representative = the median-loss history.
   - **Speed and correctness of the simulation:**
     - numba njit with np.random.Generator passed in, which is bit-identical to plain Python;
     - MODEL_NO_JIT=1 forces plain Python.
   - **Guardrails:**
     - check_settings: unknown or missing keys, finite values, positive/non-negative values, whole numbers;
     - check_inputs: days; dt must divide a day and satisfy dt ≤ 1/(beta·gamma); N ≥ 40 required, with a warning if N < 250;
     - runtime ModelRegimeError if |lp − lf| > 1.0.
   - **Kirman ant model:** an exact stationary distribution via detailed balance, and the herding condition eps < (1−delta)/(N−1).
   - **Policy features (optional):**
     - circuit breakers: US 7/13/20% rules, 15-minute halts, scaled to model volatility;
     - policy shocks: a jump in the fundamental value on a given day;
     - experiments use paired seeds.
   - **Infrastructure:** pytest with a "slow" marker, coverage, multiprocessing Pool, which needs `if __name__=="__main__"` and a real script file (stdin scripts hang).
   - **Data:** yfinance data; FRED (DFF, FEDFUNDS, DGS10, USREC); stocks are price-only (split-adjusted, not dividend-adjusted).
   - **Figures:** dataviz palette — ink #0b0b0b, blue #2a78d6, orange #eb6834, aqua #1baf7a, muted #898781 — validated as colorblind-safe.

3. Files and Code Sections:

   **Layout (repo root):** CLAUDE.md, main.py, make_figures.py, calibrated_params.json, herding/, tests/, analysis/ (with history/), data/, figures/, paper/, notes/, journal/, scratch/ (gitignored), .claude/ (hooks/save_journal.py, settings.json, skills/learn-with-ai-tutor, skills/test-every-function).

   **herding/model.py**
   - Defaults:
     ```
     P = dict(N=500, v1=3.0, v2=2.0, beta=50.0, tc=0.1, gamma=0.1, a1=0.6, a2=2.0, a3=0.5, R=0.0004, s=0.75, sigma_news=0.01, pf0=10.0, dt=0.02, min_chartists=4, tau=0.2)
     ```
   - Constants: U_MAX = 30, N_STABLE = 250, MAX_MISPRICING = 1.0, POSITIVE / NON_NEGATIVE / WHOLE.
   - Guardrails: class ModelRegimeError, check_settings, check_inputs, initial_counts(N, herding, min_chartists) (each type starts at max(N//20, m//2)).
   - Kernel:
     ```
     _run_impl(g, days, steps, herding, N, nf, npl, nmi, m2, mF, lp, v1, v2, beta, tc, gamma, a1, a2, a3, R, s, sigma, tau, max_mis, cb1, cb2, cb3, halt_steps, shock)
     ```
     It returns (lp, lf, frac, halts, low, max_step, status, day). It is numba-jitted when USE_JIT.
   - check_breakers(breakers) takes dict(levels=(l1, l2, l3), halt_minutes=m). check_shocks(shocks, days) takes {day: fraction > −1}.
   - Entry points:
     - `simulate_full(days, herding=True, p=P, seed=None, max_mispricing=MAX_MISPRICING, breakers=None, shocks=None)` returns a dict with r, frac, lp, lf, halts, low, max_step.
     - `simulate(days, herding=True, p=P, seed=None, paths=False, max_mispricing=..., breakers=None, shocks=None)` returns (r, frac) or (r, frac, lp, lf).

   **herding/stats.py**
   - Helpers: _returns, _standardize. Both raise ValueError on empty, NaN or constant input.
   - Measures: hill_alpha(r, tail=0.05) drops zeros and requires 0 < tail < 1; kurtosis; ccdf; acf(r, lags), computed with corrcoef; tail_share(r, k=4).
   - stylized_facts(r) returns keys kurtosis, alpha_5pct, alpha_1pct, share_4sd, ac_r_1, ac_r_2, ac_r_2to10, ac_abs_1, ac_abs_20, ac_abs_50, ac_abs_100.

   **herding/market_data.py**
   - Paths: ROOT = parent.parent; MARKETS = {spx: data/spx_daily.csv (1950–), spx_1928: data/spx_daily_1928.csv, ndx: data/ndx_daily.csv}; STOCKS = data/stocks.
   - Functions: load_prices(path) with checks; load_spx; spx_returns; returns(market); stock_tickers(); stock_returns(t); black_monday(returns).

   **herding/kirman.py**

# Results: Can herding explain market crashes?

All figures are made by `python3 make_figures.py` (about 1 minute). Every model check
uses **held-out seeds** that the calibration never saw, so the model is not graded on
its own homework. Colors mean the same thing in every figure:

| Color | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Black | the real market (S&P 500 or other real data) |
| Blue | the **calibrated** Lux–Marchesi model (settings fitted to the S&P 500) |
| Orange | the model with the **original 1999 paper settings** |
| Aqua | the model with **no chartists** (bell-curve news only; the base case) |
| Gray dashes | reference lines (bell curve, slope −3) |

**Key vocabulary**
- **Fundamentalist:** a trader who buys when the price is below the company's true value and sells when it's above.
- **Chartist:** a trader who ignores value and follows the trend and the crowd.
- **Fat tail:** big days happen far more often than a bell curve says.
- **Tail exponent α:** how fast big days become rare; smaller α means more crashes, and real markets have α ≈ 3.
- **Volatility clustering / memory:** big moves come in bunches, so a wild day predicts more wild days later.
- **Percentile:** where the real value falls among 20 simulated histories. 50% is perfectly typical; below 5% or above 95% is unusual.

---

## Fig 1. The S&P 500's fingerprint vs the calibrated model
![](fig1_fingerprint.png)

**Question:** does the real S&P 500 (1950–2026) look like a typical history of the model?

**How to read it:** each of the 10 panels is one measure of how a market behaves.
- The **blue bar** spans 90% of 20 simulated 77-year histories, and the blue dot is their median.
- The **black diamond** is the real S&P 500.
- The **orange X** is the paper's original settings.

**Result:**
- The real S&P sits inside the calibrated model's typical range on **9 of 10** measures.
- The one miss is the **2-day return correlation**: after a big move, the model tends to partly reverse it two days later more than the real market does. This is the model's known weak spot.
- The paper settings miss badly on volatility memory at 20, 50 and 100 days. They forget wild periods almost immediately.

## Fig 2. Fat tails
![](fig2_tails.png)

**Question:** are big days more common than a bell curve predicts, and does herding cause it?

**How to read it:** this is a log-log plot, which turns a power law into a straight line. The x-axis is the size of a daily move in standard deviations; the y-axis is the share of days with an even bigger move.

**Result:**
- The real S&P and the calibrated model both run along the **slope −3 line**, the inverse cubic law found by Gopikrishnan et al. (1998). Moves are 8 times rarer each time their size doubles.
- With **no chartists**, the model's tail drops away exactly like the bell curve.
- **This is the proposal's central check:** the news is a bell curve in both runs, so the fat tail comes from the traders, not the news.
- Black Monday 1987 (23 standard deviations) sits at the far right. The model produces days of 20+ standard deviations too.

## Fig 3. Volatility clustering and predictability
![](fig3_memory.png)

**Left, volatility memory:** does a big move today predict big moves k days later?
- The real S&P still "remembers" a wild period after 100 days (correlation about 0.09).
- The calibrated model's median follows the S&P almost exactly.
- The paper settings forget within about 30 days.

**Right, return correlation:** does today's *direction* predict tomorrow's?
- In the real market, no: it's about 0. If direction were predictable, traders would trade the pattern away.
- The model has a small reversal over days 2–5, the same weak spot as in Fig 1.

## Fig 4. How the calibrated model makes a crash
![](fig4_mechanism.png)

**How to read it:** the same 700 days of one typical held-out history, shown in three panels.

**Result, the crash cycle:**
1. A few traders become chartists, and each one makes it easier to recruit more. Their share snowballs from about 2% to nearly 100% (panel ②).
2. With almost no fundamentalists left, nothing pulls the price back toward its value. The price swings up to 30% away from it (panel ③), and returns explode to 20 standard deviations (panel ①).
3. Once the price is far from its value, betting on its return looks profitable. Traders drift back to being fundamentalists, and calm returns.

**This answers the project question:** in this model, crashes come from *herding into the trend-following strategy* (copying strategy), not from bad news.

## Fig 5. Kirman's ant model (the proposal's first check)
![](fig5_kirman.png)

**Setup:** 100 ants choose between two identical food sources. Each step, one ant either switches on its own (probability ε) or is recruited by another ant.

**Result:**
- When spontaneous switching is rarer than recruitment (left), the ants **herd**: most of them sit at one source, then the whole crowd flips.
- Otherwise (right), they split about 50/50.
- In the bottom panels, the time the simulation spends at each state (bars) matches **Kirman's exact formula** (line), with a mismatch of only 0.020 and 0.004.
- This is the recruitment mechanism that Lux–Marchesi uses for traders.

## Fig 6. Out-of-sample test: data the calibration never saw
![](fig6_out_of_sample.png)

**How to read it:** each row is a real data series and each column a measure. A cell is the real data's percentile among 20 model histories. Gray means typical; strong blue or red with a bold number means unusual. With 10 measures and a 5–95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by pure chance.

**Result:**
- Only 6 of 230 cells are unusual, fewer than chance alone would produce.
- The **Nasdaq-100** looks typical on every measure, and so does the **S&P 500 from 1928**, including the 1929 crash and the Great Depression, except one cell (the reversal again).
- The **20 stocks with market beta 0.9–1.1** (stocks that move about 1-for-1 with the market) mostly look typical. Some show more extreme days than the model. That's expected: single companies also get company-specific news (earnings surprises, lawsuits) that a whole-market model doesn't have.

**Caveat:** the stocks are companies that are large *today*, so failed firms are missing (survivorship bias).

## Fig 7. Policy experiment 1: circuit breakers
![](fig7_circuit_breakers.png)

**Setup:**
- Each dot is one 77-year history, run twice with **identical randomness**: once without and once with US-style circuit breakers. The real rules since 2013 are 15-minute pauses at −7% and −13% and a full-day close at −20%; here they're scaled ×1.34 to match the model's volatility.
- Dots below the dashed line mean breakers helped.
- Dots exactly on the line are histories where no breaker ever fired.

**Result:**
- Breakers lower the **worst single day** in 14 of 20 histories, by about 10%.
- But the **worst 5-day and 20-day falls** barely change: only 11 of 20 histories improve over 20 days, close to a coin flip.
- Pauses **spread a crash over more days rather than prevent it**, because they don't change why traders crowd into trend-following.
- This agrees with the SEC staff's finding that the 1997 halts did not clearly stabilize prices.

## Fig 8. Policy experiment 2: a policy surprise (like an unexpected rate hike)
![](fig8_policy_shocks.png)

**Setup:**
- 200 histories, each run twice with identical randomness: with and without a one-time surprise that cuts the company's true value by 10%.
- The surprise stands in for real events such as an unexpected Fed rate hike, the 1930 tariffs, or the 2011 US credit downgrade.

**Result:**
- In a **calm market** (under 10% chartists), the price simply falls 10%, exactly the size of the surprise.
- In a **crowded market** (over 30% chartists), trend-chasers pile on and the fall **overshoots by up to about 25%**: a 10% surprise becomes about a 12.5% fall.
- **In this model, the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.** The same news is harmless in a calm market and amplified in a crowded one.

---

## Honest limitations
1. **Two-day reversal.** After a big move the model slightly reverses it over the next 2–5 days, and the real market does not (Figs 1, 3, 6).
2. **One market, no individual companies.** The model can't produce company-specific shocks or insider trading.
3. **Changes from the 1999 paper.** Log prices, a faster market maker, and minimum group sizes were needed to fix bugs, so the model is not the paper's exact equations.
4. **Large differences between histories.** Even with the same settings, one 77-year history can be calm and another full of crashes. A single history (including the real one) is weak evidence on its own; that's why every check here uses 20.
5. **Policy experiments are stylized.** Breaker timing rules are simplified (no 3:25 pm cutoff), and a "policy surprise" is a one-time jump in value, not a model of the Fed.

"""Tests for main.py: the end-to-end comparison runs and saves its figure."""
import numpy as np
import pytest

from conftest import ROOT
from herding import calibrate
import main
from herding import model
from herding import stats


def test_main_runs_end_to_end(tmp_path, capsys):
    out = tmp_path / "draft.png"
    real, herd, base = main.main(out=out, histories=3, days=3000)
    text = capsys.readouterr().out
    assert out.exists() and out.stat().st_size > 50_000           # a real figure
    assert "-20.5%" in text and "23.0 standard deviations" in text  # Black Monday line
    assert len(herd) == len(base) == 3000 and len(real) > 19_000
    assert "typical history: seed" in text and "no-chartist base case" in text


def test_main_table_has_every_fact_and_columns(tmp_path, capsys):
    main.main(out=tmp_path / "f.png", histories=3, days=3000)
    text = capsys.readouterr().out
    lines = text.split("simulated histories")[1].splitlines()[1:]
    assert all(c in lines[0] for c in ["S&P 500", "calibrated", "S&P pct", "paper set"])
    for fact in stats.stylized_facts(np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(500)):
        assert any(l.startswith(fact) for l in lines), fact


def test_plotted_history_is_the_median_mismatch_one(tmp_path):
    # main must plot the typical history, not a cherry-picked best one
    _, herd, _ = main.main(out=tmp_path / "f.png", histories=5, days=3000)
    runs, facts = main.ensemble(calibrate.load(), main.SEEDS[:5], days=3000)
    target = stats.stylized_facts(main.data.spx_returns().values)
    i = calibrate.representative(facts, target)
    assert np.array_equal(herd, runs[i])


def test_ensemble_table_flags_unusual_facts():
    target = {"x": 10.0}
    sims = [{"x": float(v)} for v in range(20)]          # S&P at the 50th percentile
    assert "unusual" not in main.ensemble_table(target, sims, sims)
    assert "unusual" in main.ensemble_table({"x": 99.0}, sims, sims)


def test_run_model_drops_burn_in():
    r, f = main.run_model(seed=4, days=500)
    full, _ = model.simulate(500 + main.BURN, seed=4)
    assert np.array_equal(r, full[main.BURN:]) and len(f) == 500


def test_main_histories_are_held_out_from_calibration():
    # Bug fix: the "is the S&P typical?" table must use seeds the calibration
    # never scored, or it overstates the fit
    assert set(main.SEEDS).isdisjoint(calibrate.CALIBRATION_SEEDS)
    assert len(main.SEEDS) >= main.HISTORIES
