97	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 2
98	@styled
99	def fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base):
100	    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
101	    pooled = np.concatenate([(r - r.mean()) / r.std() for r in cal_runs])
102	    for r, lab, c, ls in [(spx, "S&P 500 (real)", INK, "-"), (pooled, "calibrated model (20 histories)", BLUE, "-"),
103	                          (base, "no chartists (bell-curve news only)", AQUA, "-")]:
104	        z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
105	        ax.loglog(z, cc, ls, color=c, label=lab)
106	        ax.annotate(lab.split(" (")[0], (z[-1], cc[-1]), xytext=(5, 0), textcoords="offset points",
107	                    fontsize=8.5, color=INK, va="center")
108	    g = np.linspace(1, 9, 100)
109	    ax.loglog(g, 2 * norm.sf(g), "--", color=MUTED, lw=1.5, label="Gaussian (bell curve)")
110	    ax.loglog(g, 0.6 * g ** -3.0, ":", color=MUTED, lw=1.8, label="slope −3: inverse cubic law")
111	    ax.set_xlim(0.8, 40); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
112	    ax.set_xlabel("size of daily move, in standard deviations (log scale)")
113	    ax.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move (log scale)")
114	    ax.set_title("Fig 2. Fat tails: big days are far more common than a bell curve predicts")
115	    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8.5)
116	    i = np.argmin(spx)
117	    ax.annotate("Black Monday 1987\n(23 std)", (abs(spx[i]) / spx.std(), 1 / len(spx)),
118	                xytext=(-110, 25), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8.5, color=INK,
119	                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED))
120	    save(fig, "fig2_tails.png",
121	         "On log-log axes a power law is a straight line. The real S&P and the calibrated model both "
122	         "follow the slope −3 line (the inverse cubic law, Gopikrishnan et al. 1998) over two orders of "
123	         "magnitude. With no chartists, the model's tail bends down exactly like the Gaussian: herding "
124	         "is what creates the fat tail.")
125	
126	
127	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 3
128	@styled
129	def fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
130	    lags = np.arange(1, 101)
131	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[2, 1]))
132	    for ax, lg, f, title in [(axes[0], lags, np.abs, "Volatility memory: does a big move predict big moves later?"),
133	                             (axes[1], lags[:10], lambda x: x, "Return correlation: does today's direction predict tomorrow's?")]:
134	        cal = np.array([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in cal_runs])
135	        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(cal, [5, 50, 95], axis=0)
136	        ax.fill_between(lg, lo, hi, color=BLUE_LIGHT, alpha=0.6, lw=0, label="calibrated model, 5-95%")
137	        ax.plot(lg, med, color=BLUE, label="calibrated model, median")
138	        ax.plot(lg, np.median([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in paper_runs], axis=0), color=ORANGE,
139	                label="paper settings, median")
140	        ax.plot(lg, stats.acf(f(spx), lg), color=INK, label="S&P 500 (real)")
141	        ax.axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
142	        ax.set_xlabel("days apart (lag)"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
143	    axes[0].set_ylabel("correlation")
144	    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
145	    fig.suptitle("Fig 3. Volatility clustering: the calibrated model remembers wild periods as long as the market does",
146	                 y=1.03, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
147	    fig.tight_layout()
148	    save(fig, "fig3_memory.png",
149	         "Left: correlation between the SIZE of moves k days apart. The S&P still remembers a wild "
150	         "period after 100 days; the paper settings forget within ~30 days; the calibrated model tracks "
151	         "the S&P. Right: correlation of DIRECTION. The real market is unpredictable (≈0). The model "
152	         "has a small 2-day reversal (the S&P is outside its typical range here: its known weak spot).")
153	
154	
155	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 4
156	@styled
157	def fig_mechanism(p):
158	    o = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=604)
159	    r, frac, mis = o["r"][BURN:], o["frac"][BURN:], (o["lp"] - o["lf"])[BURN + 1:]
160	    i = int(np.argmin(r))
161	    w = slice(max(0, i - 400), min(len(r), i + 300))
162	    d = np.arange(len(r))[w] - i
163	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
164	    axes[0].plot(d, r[w] / r.std(), color=INK, lw=0.8)
165	    axes[0].set_ylabel("daily return\n(std units)")
166	    axes[0].set_title("① Returns: calm, then a burst of huge moves (the crash)", loc="left")
167	    axes[1].fill_between(d, 0, frac[w] * 100, color=BLUE, alpha=0.8, lw=0)
168	    axes[1].set_ylabel("chartists\n(% of traders)")
169	    axes[1].set_title("② Chartist share: traders crowd into trend-following, recruiting each other", loc="left")
170	    axes[2].plot(d, mis[w] * 100, color=ORANGE)
171	    axes[2].axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
172	    axes[2].set_ylabel("price vs value\n(% mispricing)")
173	    axes[2].set_title("③ Mispricing: with few fundamentalists left, nothing anchors the price", loc="left")
174	    axes[2].set_xlabel("days relative to the worst day of this history")
175	    for ax in axes:
176	        ax.axvline(0, color=RED, lw=1, ls="--")
177	    fig.suptitle("Fig 4. How the calibrated model makes a crash (a typical held-out history, seed 604)",
178	                 y=1.0, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
179	    fig.tight_layout()
180	    save(fig, "fig4_mechanism.png",
181	         "The same days in three panels. The crash (red line) comes when the share of chartists surges: "
182	         "each chartist makes it easier to recruit more (Kirman-style crowding), so fundamentalists "
183	         "dwindle and the price swings far from its value. As mispricing grows, betting on the price "
184	         "returning looks profitable, traders switch back to fundamentalist, and calm returns.")
185	
186	
187	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 5
188	@styled
189	def fig_kirman():
190	    cases = [("herding: ε < (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.002, delta=0.01)),
191	             ("no herding: ε > (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.05, delta=0.01))]
192	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7))
193	    for col, (name, kw) in enumerate(cases):
194	        k = kirman.simulate(**kw, steps=40_000_000, seed=1)
195	        show = k[:5_000_000:2_000]                   # first 5M steps, for readability
196	        axes[0, col].plot(np.arange(len(show)) * 2_000 / 1e6, show, color=BLUE, lw=0.8)
197	        axes[0, col].set_ylim(0, 100); axes[0, col].set_ylabel("ants at source A")
198	        axes[0, col].set_xlabel("steps (millions; first 5M of 40M shown)"); axes[0, col].set_title(name)
199	        hist = np.bincount(k, minlength=101) / len(k)
200	        axes[1, col].bar(np.arange(101), hist, width=0.9, color=BLUE_LIGHT, label="simulation (40M steps)")
201	        axes[1, col].plot(np.arange(101), kirman.stationary(**kw), color=INK, lw=1.8,
202	                          label="Kirman's exact answer")
203	        tv = 0.5 * np.abs(hist - kirman.stationary(**kw)).sum()
204	        axes[1, col].set_xlabel("ants at source A"); axes[1, col].set_ylabel("share of time")
205	        axes[1, col].text(0.5, 0.55 if col == 0 else 0.08, f"mismatch (total variation) = {tv:.3f}",
206	                          transform=axes[1, col].transAxes, ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
207	        axes[1, col].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper center" if col == 0 else "upper left")
208	    fig.suptitle("Fig 5. Kirman's ant model reproduces his exact math: herding makes the crowd flip all at once",
209	                 y=1.01, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
210	    fig.tight_layout()
211	    save(fig, "fig5_kirman.png",
212	         "100 ants choose between two identical food sources (N=100, δ=0.01). Left: when spontaneous "
213	         "switching ε is rarer than recruitment, ants herd at one source and then flip en masse. Right: "
214	         "otherwise they split about 50/50. Bottom: time spent at each state (bars) matches the exact "
215	         "long-run answer from detailed balance (line). This is the herding mechanism inside Lux-Marchesi.")
216	
217	
218	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 6
219	@styled
220	def fig_out_of_sample(pool, p):
221	    rows, names = [], []
222	    series = [("S&P 500 1950- (held-out seeds)", market_data.returns("spx").values),
223	              ("S&P 500 1928- (Great Depression)", market_data.returns("spx_1928").values),
224	              ("Nasdaq-100 1985-", market_data.returns("ndx").values)]
225	    series += [(f"stock {t}", market_data.stock_returns(t).values) for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
226	    cache = {}
227	    for name, r in series:
228	        n = len(r) if not name.startswith("stock") else 6700
229	        if n not in cache:
230	            cache[n] = [stats.stylized_facts(x) for x in ensemble(pool, p, range(700, 720), n)]
231	        pct = calibrate.percentiles(stats.stylized_facts(r), cache[n], calibrate.TARGETS)
232	        rows.append([pct[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS]); names.append(name)
233	    m = np.array(rows)
234	    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 10))
235	    from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
236	    cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", ["#256abf", "#9ec5f4", "#f0efec", "#f2a3a2", "#c53a39"])
237	    im = ax.imshow(m, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
238	    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(m):
239	        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
240	                color=INK, fontweight="bold" if not 5 <= v <= 95 else "normal")
241	    ax.set_xticks(range(len(calibrate.TARGETS)), [LABELS[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS],
242	                  rotation=35, ha="right", fontsize=8.5)
243	    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names, fontsize=8.5); ax.grid(False)
244	    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.6)
245	    cb.set_label("percentile of real data among 20 model histories\n(50 = perfectly typical; <5 or >95 = unusual)")
246	    ax.set_title("Fig 6. Out-of-sample: data the calibration never saw, scored against the model")
247	    unusual = int(np.sum((m < 5) | (m > 95)))
248	    save(fig, "fig6_out_of_sample.png",
249	         f"Gray cells are typical; strong blue/red cells (bold numbers) are unusual. With 10 measures and a "
250	         f"5-95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by chance alone. {unusual} of {m.size} "
251	         f"cells are unusual. The Nasdaq-100 and the 1928-2026 S&P (including the Great Depression) look "
252	         f"typical; stocks show more >4-std days than the model, because single companies also get "
253	         f"company-specific news (earnings surprises) that a whole-market model does not have.")
254	
255	
256	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 7
257	def _breaker_pair(args):
258	    p, seed, levels = args
259	    out = []
260	    for b in (None, dict(levels=levels, halt_minutes=15)):
261	        r = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=seed, breakers=b)["r"][BURN:]
262	        out.append([worst_fall(r, k) for k in (1, 5, 20)])
263	    return out
264	
265	
266	@styled
267	def fig_breakers(pool, p, cal_runs, spx):
268	    rules, scale = experiments.scaled_breakers(np.median([r.std() for r in cal_runs]), spx.std())
269	    res = np.array(pool.map(_breaker_pair, [(p, s, rules["levels"]) for s in range(3000, 3020)]))
270	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.8))
271	    for j, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, ["worst single day", "worst 5-day fall", "worst 20-day fall"])):
272	        off, on = np.expm1(-res[:, 0, j]) * -100, np.expm1(-res[:, 1, j]) * -100
273	        top = max(off.max(), on.max()) * 1.08
274	        ax.plot([0, top], [0, top], color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
275	        ax.scatter(off, on, s=60, color=BLUE, edgecolor="#fcfcfb", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
276	        lower, higher = int(np.sum(on < off - 1e-9)), int(np.sum(on > off + 1e-9))
277	        ax.set_title(f"{name}\nlower with breakers in {lower}/20, higher in {higher}/20", fontsize=10)
278	        ax.set_xlabel("fall without breakers (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("fall with breakers (%)")
279	        ax.set_xlim(0, top); ax.set_ylim(0, top)
280	        ax.text(0.05 * top, 0.9 * top, "below the line =\nbreakers helped", fontsize=8, color=SECOND)
281	    fig.suptitle("Fig 7. Circuit breakers soften the worst day but barely change multi-day crashes",
282	                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
283	    fig.tight_layout()
284	    save(fig, "fig7_circuit_breakers.png",
285	         f"Each dot is one 77-year history run twice with identical randomness: without and with US-style "
286	         f"circuit breakers (15-min pauses at −7% and −13%, close at −20%, scaled ×{scale:.2f} to the "
287	         f"model's volatility). Dots on the dashed line: no breaker ever fired. Breakers cut the worst "
288	         f"single day (~10%), but the 5- and 20-day falls barely move: pauses spread a crash over more "
289	         f"days rather than prevent it. This matches SEC findings on 1997 (halts did not clearly stabilize prices).")
290	
291	
292	# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 8
293	def _shock_pair(args):
294	    p, seed = args
295	    a = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed)
296	    b = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed, shocks={1000: -0.10})
297	    return a["frac"][999], (b["lp"] - a["lp"])[1000:1061]
298	
299	
300	@styled
301	def fig_shocks(pool, p):
302	    res = pool.map(_shock_pair, [(p, s) for s in range(5000, 5200)])
303	    frac = np.array([x[0] for x in res]); paths = np.array([x[1] for x in res])
304	    resp = paths / np.log(0.9)                       # 1.0 = moved exactly by the shock
305	    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))
306	    for lo, hi, c, lab in [(0, 0.1, "#86b6ef", "calm market (<10% chartists)"),
307	                           (0.3, 1.01, "#184f95", "crowded market (>30% chartists)")]:
308	        sel = (frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)
309	        axes[0].plot(np.arange(61), np.median(resp[sel], axis=0), color=c, label=f"{lab}, n={sel.sum()}")
310	        axes[0].fill_between(np.arange(61), np.percentile(resp[sel], 10, axis=0),
311	                             np.percentile(resp[sel], 90, axis=0), color=c, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
312	    axes[0].axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
313	    axes[0].set_xlabel("days after a surprise that cuts value 10%")
314	    axes[0].set_ylabel("price fall ÷ shock size\n(1.0 = moved exactly by the shock)")
315	    axes[0].set_title("Price response (median, 10-90% band)"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
316	    bins = [(0, 0.1), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 1.01)]
317	    over = [resp[(frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)].max(axis=1) for lo, hi in bins]

"""Make every results figure (figures/fig*.png) for the project write-up.

Run:  python3 make_figures.py      (~1-2 min with numba)
All model checks use held-out seeds the calibration never saw.
Colors (validated colorblind-safe): S&P/real data = ink, calibrated = blue,
paper settings = orange, no chartists = aqua, references = muted gray dashes.
"""
from multiprocessing import Pool

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

from herding import calibrate, experiments, kirman, market_data, model, stats
from herding.experiments import BURN, DAYS, worst_fall

FIG = market_data.ROOT / "figures"
INK, SECOND, MUTED, GRID = "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#e1e0d9"
BLUE, ORANGE, AQUA, RED = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#e34948"
BLUE_LIGHT = "#b7d3f6"
HELD_OUT = range(600, 620)                       # never used by the calibration
LABELS = dict(alpha_5pct="tail exponent α (5% tail)", alpha_1pct="tail exponent α (1% tail)",
              share_4sd="share of days beyond 4 std", ac_r_1="return correlation, 1 day",
              ac_r_2="return correlation, 2 days", ac_r_2to10="return correlation, days 2-10",
              ac_abs_1="volatility memory, 1 day", ac_abs_20="volatility memory, 20 days",
              ac_abs_50="volatility memory, 50 days", ac_abs_100="volatility memory, 100 days")

STYLE = {   # applied only while a figure is drawn (see styled), never globally
    "font.family": "sans-serif", "font.size": 10, "axes.titlesize": 11,
    "axes.titleweight": "bold", "axes.edgecolor": "#c3c2b7", "axes.labelcolor": SECOND,
    "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED, "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID,
    "grid.linewidth": 0.6, "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False,
    "figure.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "axes.facecolor": "#fcfcfb", "legend.frameon": False,
    "lines.linewidth": 2, "savefig.dpi": 150, "savefig.bbox": "tight"}


def styled(fn):
    """Draw a figure with STYLE without changing matplotlib's global settings."""
    import functools

    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        with plt.rc_context(STYLE):
            return fn(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper


def save(fig, name, caption):
    fig.text(0.01, -0.02, caption, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=8.5, color=SECOND, wrap=True)
    fig.savefig(FIG / name)
    plt.close(fig)
    print("saved", name)


def ensemble(pool, p, seeds=HELD_OUT, days=DAYS, herding=True):
    return experiments.ensemble(p, seeds, days, herding, pool=pool)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 1
@styled
def fig_fingerprint(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
    target = stats.stylized_facts(spx)
    cal = [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in cal_runs]
    paper = [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in paper_runs]
    pct = calibrate.percentiles(target, cal, calibrate.TARGETS)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(15, 5.6))
    for ax, k in zip(axes.flat, calibrate.TARGETS):
        v = np.array([f[k] for f in cal])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(v, [5, 50, 95])
        ax.plot([0, 0], [lo, hi], color=BLUE, lw=6, solid_capstyle="round", alpha=0.35)
        ax.plot(0, med, "o", color=BLUE, ms=8, label="calibrated model (median, 5-95%)")
        ax.plot(0.25, np.median([f[k] for f in paper]), "X", color=ORANGE, ms=9,
                label="paper settings (median)")
        ax.plot(-0.25, target[k], "D", color=INK, ms=8, label="S&P 500 1950-2026")
        ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 0.6); ax.set_xticks([])
        flag = "typical" if 5 <= pct[k] <= 95 else "UNUSUAL"
        ax.set_title(f"{LABELS[k]}\nS&P percentile {pct[k]:.0f}% ({flag})", fontsize=9.5,
                     color=INK if flag == "typical" else RED)
        ylo, yhi = ax.get_ylim()
        ax.set_ylim(ylo - 0.06 * (yhi - ylo), yhi + 0.06 * (yhi - ylo))
    h, l = axes.flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(h, l, loc="upper center", ncol=3, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.04))
    fig.suptitle("Fig 1. The S&P 500's fingerprint vs 20 held-out histories of the calibrated model",
                 y=1.12, fontsize=13, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    n_typ = sum(5 <= v <= 95 for v in pct.values())
    save(fig, "fig1_fingerprint.png",
         f"Each panel is one measure. Blue bar: the range covering 90% of 20 simulated 77-year histories "
         f"(seeds 600-619, never used in calibration); blue dot: their median. Black diamond: the real "
         f"S&P 500. Orange X: the original paper settings. The S&P falls inside the model's typical "
         f"range on {n_typ} of 10 measures; the paper settings miss volatility memory badly.")
    return pct


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 2
@styled
def fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.5))
    pooled = np.concatenate([(r - r.mean()) / r.std() for r in cal_runs])
    for r, lab, c, ls in [(spx, "S&P 500 (real)", INK, "-"), (pooled, "calibrated model (20 histories)", BLUE, "-"),
                          (base, "no chartists (bell-curve news only)", AQUA, "-")]:
        z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
        ax.loglog(z, cc, ls, color=c, label=lab)
        ax.annotate(lab.split(" (")[0], (z[-1], cc[-1]), xytext=(5, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                    fontsize=8.5, color=INK, va="center")
    g = np.linspace(1, 9, 100)
    ax.loglog(g, 2 * norm.sf(g), "--", color=MUTED, lw=1.5, label="Gaussian (bell curve)")
    ax.loglog(g, 0.6 * g ** -3.0, ":", color=MUTED, lw=1.8, label="slope −3: inverse cubic law")
    ax.set_xlim(0.8, 40); ax.set_ylim(1e-5, 1)
    ax.set_xlabel("size of daily move, in standard deviations (log scale)")
    ax.set_ylabel("share of days with a bigger move (log scale)")
    ax.set_title("Fig 2. Fat tails: big days are far more common than a bell curve predicts")
    ax.legend(loc="lower left", fontsize=8.5)
    i = np.argmin(spx)
    ax.annotate("Black Monday 1987\n(23 std)", (abs(spx[i]) / spx.std(), 1 / len(spx)),
                xytext=(-110, 25), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=8.5, color=INK,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED))
    save(fig, "fig2_tails.png",
         "On log-log axes a power law is a straight line. The real S&P and the calibrated model both "
         "follow the slope −3 line (the inverse cubic law, Gopikrishnan et al. 1998) over two orders of "
         "magnitude. With no chartists, the model's tail bends down exactly like the Gaussian: herding "
         "is what creates the fat tail.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 3
@styled
def fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs):
    lags = np.arange(1, 101)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[2, 1]))
    for ax, lg, f, title in [(axes[0], lags, np.abs, "Volatility memory: does a big move predict big moves later?"),
                             (axes[1], lags[:10], lambda x: x, "Return correlation: does today's direction predict tomorrow's?")]:
        cal = np.array([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in cal_runs])
        lo, med, hi = np.percentile(cal, [5, 50, 95], axis=0)
        ax.fill_between(lg, lo, hi, color=BLUE_LIGHT, alpha=0.6, lw=0, label="calibrated model, 5-95%")
        ax.plot(lg, med, color=BLUE, label="calibrated model, median")
        ax.plot(lg, np.median([stats.acf(f(r), lg) for r in paper_runs], axis=0), color=ORANGE,
                label="paper settings, median")
        ax.plot(lg, stats.acf(f(spx), lg), color=INK, label="S&P 500 (real)")
        ax.axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
        ax.set_xlabel("days apart (lag)"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("correlation")
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 3. Volatility clustering: the calibrated model remembers wild periods as long as the market does",
                 y=1.03, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig3_memory.png",
         "Left: correlation between the SIZE of moves k days apart. The S&P still remembers a wild "
         "period after 100 days; the paper settings forget within ~30 days; the calibrated model tracks "
         "the S&P. Right: correlation of DIRECTION. The real market is unpredictable (≈0). The model "
         "has a small 2-day reversal (the S&P is outside its typical range here: its known weak spot).")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 4
@styled
def fig_mechanism(p):
    o = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=604)
    r, frac, mis = o["r"][BURN:], o["frac"][BURN:], (o["lp"] - o["lf"])[BURN + 1:]
    i = int(np.argmin(r))
    w = slice(max(0, i - 400), min(len(r), i + 300))
    d = np.arange(len(r))[w] - i
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True)
    axes[0].plot(d, r[w] / r.std(), color=INK, lw=0.8)
    axes[0].set_ylabel("daily return\n(std units)")
    axes[0].set_title("① Returns: calm, then a burst of huge moves (the crash)", loc="left")
    axes[1].fill_between(d, 0, frac[w] * 100, color=BLUE, alpha=0.8, lw=0)
    axes[1].set_ylabel("chartists\n(% of traders)")
    axes[1].set_title("② Chartist share: traders crowd into trend-following, recruiting each other", loc="left")
    axes[2].plot(d, mis[w] * 100, color=ORANGE)
    axes[2].axhline(0, color="#c3c2b7", lw=1)
    axes[2].set_ylabel("price vs value\n(% mispricing)")
    axes[2].set_title("③ Mispricing: with few fundamentalists left, nothing anchors the price", loc="left")
    axes[2].set_xlabel("days relative to the worst day of this history")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.axvline(0, color=RED, lw=1, ls="--")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 4. How the calibrated model makes a crash (a typical held-out history, seed 604)",
                 y=1.0, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig4_mechanism.png",
         "The same days in three panels. The crash (red line) comes when the share of chartists surges: "
         "each chartist makes it easier to recruit more (Kirman-style crowding), so fundamentalists "
         "dwindle and the price swings far from its value. As mispricing grows, betting on the price "
         "returning looks profitable, traders switch back to fundamentalist, and calm returns.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 5
@styled
def fig_kirman():
    cases = [("herding: ε < (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.002, delta=0.01)),
             ("no herding: ε > (1−δ)/(N−1)", dict(N=100, eps=0.05, delta=0.01))]
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7))
    for col, (name, kw) in enumerate(cases):
        k = kirman.simulate(**kw, steps=40_000_000, seed=1)
        show = k[:5_000_000:2_000]                   # first 5M steps, for readability
        axes[0, col].plot(np.arange(len(show)) * 2_000 / 1e6, show, color=BLUE, lw=0.8)
        axes[0, col].set_ylim(0, 100); axes[0, col].set_ylabel("ants at source A")
        axes[0, col].set_xlabel("steps (millions; first 5M of 40M shown)"); axes[0, col].set_title(name)
        hist = np.bincount(k, minlength=101) / len(k)
        axes[1, col].bar(np.arange(101), hist, width=0.9, color=BLUE_LIGHT, label="simulation (40M steps)")
        axes[1, col].plot(np.arange(101), kirman.stationary(**kw), color=INK, lw=1.8,
                          label="Kirman's exact answer")
        tv = 0.5 * np.abs(hist - kirman.stationary(**kw)).sum()
        axes[1, col].set_xlabel("ants at source A"); axes[1, col].set_ylabel("share of time")
        axes[1, col].text(0.5, 0.55 if col == 0 else 0.08, f"mismatch (total variation) = {tv:.3f}",
                          transform=axes[1, col].transAxes, ha="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
        axes[1, col].legend(fontsize=8.5, loc="upper center" if col == 0 else "upper left")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 5. Kirman's ant model reproduces his exact math: herding makes the crowd flip all at once",
                 y=1.01, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig5_kirman.png",
         "100 ants choose between two identical food sources (N=100, δ=0.01). Left: when spontaneous "
         "switching ε is rarer than recruitment, ants herd at one source and then flip en masse. Right: "
         "otherwise they split about 50/50. Bottom: time spent at each state (bars) matches the exact "
         "long-run answer from detailed balance (line). This is the herding mechanism inside Lux-Marchesi.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 6
@styled
def fig_out_of_sample(pool, p):
    rows, names = [], []
    series = [("S&P 500 1950- (held-out seeds)", market_data.returns("spx").values),
              ("S&P 500 1928- (Great Depression)", market_data.returns("spx_1928").values),
              ("Nasdaq-100 1985-", market_data.returns("ndx").values)]
    series += [(f"stock {t}", market_data.stock_returns(t).values) for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
    cache = {}
    for name, r in series:
        n = len(r) if not name.startswith("stock") else 6700
        if n not in cache:
            cache[n] = [stats.stylized_facts(x) for x in ensemble(pool, p, range(700, 720), n)]
        pct = calibrate.percentiles(stats.stylized_facts(r), cache[n], calibrate.TARGETS)
        rows.append([pct[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS]); names.append(name)
    m = np.array(rows)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 10))
    from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
    cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", ["#256abf", "#9ec5f4", "#f0efec", "#f2a3a2", "#c53a39"])
    im = ax.imshow(m, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(m):
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.5,
                color=INK, fontweight="bold" if not 5 <= v <= 95 else "normal")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(calibrate.TARGETS)), [LABELS[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS],
                  rotation=35, ha="right", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names, fontsize=8.5); ax.grid(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.6)
    cb.set_label("percentile of real data among 20 model histories\n(50 = perfectly typical; <5 or >95 = unusual)")
    ax.set_title("Fig 6. Out-of-sample: data the calibration never saw, scored against the model")
    unusual = int(np.sum((m < 5) | (m > 95)))
    save(fig, "fig6_out_of_sample.png",
         f"Gray cells are typical; strong blue/red cells (bold numbers) are unusual. With 10 measures and a "
         f"5-95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by chance alone. {unusual} of {m.size} "
         f"cells are unusual. The Nasdaq-100 and the 1928-2026 S&P (including the Great Depression) look "
         f"typical; stocks show more >4-std days than the model, because single companies also get "
         f"company-specific news (earnings surprises) that a whole-market model does not have.")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 7
def _breaker_pair(args):
    p, seed, levels = args
    out = []
    for b in (None, dict(levels=levels, halt_minutes=15)):
        r = model.simulate_full(DAYS + BURN, p=p, seed=seed, breakers=b)["r"][BURN:]
        out.append([worst_fall(r, k) for k in (1, 5, 20)])
    return out


@styled
def fig_breakers(pool, p, cal_runs, spx):
    rules, scale = experiments.scaled_breakers(np.median([r.std() for r in cal_runs]), spx.std())
    res = np.array(pool.map(_breaker_pair, [(p, s, rules["levels"]) for s in range(3000, 3020)]))
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4.8))
    for j, (ax, name) in enumerate(zip(axes, ["worst single day", "worst 5-day fall", "worst 20-day fall"])):
        off, on = np.expm1(-res[:, 0, j]) * -100, np.expm1(-res[:, 1, j]) * -100
        top = max(off.max(), on.max()) * 1.08
        ax.plot([0, top], [0, top], color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
        ax.scatter(off, on, s=60, color=BLUE, edgecolor="#fcfcfb", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)
        lower, higher = int(np.sum(on < off - 1e-9)), int(np.sum(on > off + 1e-9))
        ax.set_title(f"{name}\nlower with breakers in {lower}/20, higher in {higher}/20", fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel("fall without breakers (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("fall with breakers (%)")
        ax.set_xlim(0, top); ax.set_ylim(0, top)
        ax.text(0.05 * top, 0.9 * top, "below the line =\nbreakers helped", fontsize=8, color=SECOND)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 7. Circuit breakers soften the worst day but barely change multi-day crashes",
                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig7_circuit_breakers.png",
         f"Each dot is one 77-year history run twice with identical randomness: without and with US-style "
         f"circuit breakers (15-min pauses at −7% and −13%, close at −20%, scaled ×{scale:.2f} to the "
         f"model's volatility). Dots on the dashed line: no breaker ever fired. Breakers cut the worst "
         f"single day (~10%), but the 5- and 20-day falls barely move: pauses spread a crash over more "
         f"days rather than prevent it. This matches SEC findings on 1997 (halts did not clearly stabilize prices).")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------- figure 8
def _shock_pair(args):
    p, seed = args
    a = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed)
    b = model.simulate_full(1300, True, p, seed=seed, shocks={1000: -0.10})
    return a["frac"][999], (b["lp"] - a["lp"])[1000:1061]


@styled
def fig_shocks(pool, p):
    res = pool.map(_shock_pair, [(p, s) for s in range(5000, 5200)])
    frac = np.array([x[0] for x in res]); paths = np.array([x[1] for x in res])
    resp = paths / np.log(0.9)                       # 1.0 = moved exactly by the shock
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.8))
    for lo, hi, c, lab in [(0, 0.1, "#86b6ef", "calm market (<10% chartists)"),
                           (0.3, 1.01, "#184f95", "crowded market (>30% chartists)")]:
        sel = (frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)
        axes[0].plot(np.arange(61), np.median(resp[sel], axis=0), color=c, label=f"{lab}, n={sel.sum()}")
        axes[0].fill_between(np.arange(61), np.percentile(resp[sel], 10, axis=0),
                             np.percentile(resp[sel], 90, axis=0), color=c, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    axes[0].axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
    axes[0].set_xlabel("days after a surprise that cuts value 10%")
    axes[0].set_ylabel("price fall ÷ shock size\n(1.0 = moved exactly by the shock)")
    axes[0].set_title("Price response (median, 10-90% band)"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8.5)
    bins = [(0, 0.1), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 1.01)]
    over = [resp[(frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)].max(axis=1) for lo, hi in bins]
    names = ["<10%", "10-30%", ">30%"]
    axes[1].bar(names, [o.mean() for o in over], color=["#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#184f95"], width=0.55)
    for i, o in enumerate(over):
        axes[1].plot([i] * len(o), o, "o", color=INK, ms=3, alpha=0.35)
        axes[1].text(i, o.max() + 0.01, f"mean {o.mean():.2f}×\nmax {o.max():.2f}×", ha="center", fontsize=8.5)
    axes[1].set_ylim(0.95, max(o.max() for o in over) + 0.08)
    axes[1].set_xlabel("chartist share when the shock hits")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("largest fall ÷ shock size")
    axes[1].set_title("Overshoot depends on timing")
    fig.suptitle("Fig 8. A policy surprise is amplified only if it hits a market already full of trend-chasers",
                 y=1.04, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig8_policy_shocks.png",
         "200 histories, each run twice with identical randomness: with and without a one-time surprise "
         "that cuts the fundamental value 10% (like an unexpected rate hike). In calm markets the price "
         "simply drops 10%. In crowded markets, chartists chase the fall and the price overshoots, by up "
         "to ~25%. In this model the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.")


def main():
    FIG.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    p = calibrate.load()
    spx = market_data.spx_returns().values
    with Pool() as pool:
        cal_runs = ensemble(pool, p)
        paper_runs = ensemble(pool, model.P)
        base = experiments.history(p, seed=600, herding=False)
        fig_fingerprint(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs)
        fig_tails(spx, cal_runs, base)
        fig_memory(spx, cal_runs, paper_runs)

"""Out-of-sample test: does real data the calibration never saw look like a
typical history of the calibrated model?

Markets: S&P 500 since 1928 (Great Depression), Nasdaq-100 since 1985, and the
20 stocks with market beta near 1. For each, simulate 20 histories of the same
length and report where the real value falls (percentile; 5-95% = typical).

Run from the project folder:  python3 analysis/out_of_sample.py
"""
import sys
from multiprocessing import Pool
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent))
from herding import calibrate, experiments, market_data, stats  # noqa: E402

HISTORIES = 20


def ensemble(pool, p, days, first_seed):
    runs = experiments.ensemble(p, range(first_seed, first_seed + HISTORIES), days, pool=pool)
    return [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in runs]


def report(name, real, sims):
    pct = calibrate.percentiles(real, sims, calibrate.TARGETS)
    unusual = [k for k, v in pct.items() if not 5 <= v <= 95]
    print(f"\n{name}: S&P-style fingerprint vs {HISTORIES} model histories")
    for k in calibrate.TARGETS:
        v = np.array([s[k] for s in sims])
        flag = "  <- unusual" if k in unusual else ""
        print(f"  {k:<12}{real[k]:>8.3f}   model {np.median(v):>7.3f} "
              f"({np.percentile(v, 5):7.3f} to {np.percentile(v, 95):7.3f})  pct {pct[k]:>4.0f}%{flag}")
    return unusual


def main():
    p = calibrate.load()
    with Pool() as pool:
        results = {}
        for name in ["spx_1928", "ndx"]:
            r = market_data.returns(name).values
            results[name] = report(name, stats.stylized_facts(r), ensemble(pool, p, len(r), 1000))
        lengths = {t: len(market_data.stock_returns(t)) for t in market_data.stock_tickers()}
        sims = ensemble(pool, p, int(np.median(list(lengths.values()))), 2000)
    print("\nStocks (market beta 0.9-1.1): measures where the stock looks unusual")
    counts = {k: 0 for k in calibrate.TARGETS}
    for t in market_data.stock_tickers():
        real = stats.stylized_facts(market_data.stock_returns(t).values)
        pct = calibrate.percentiles(real, sims, calibrate.TARGETS)
        bad = [k for k, v in pct.items() if not 5 <= v <= 95]
        for k in bad:
            counts[k] += 1
        print(f"  {t:<5} {len(bad)} unusual: {', '.join(bad) if bad else '-'}")
    print("\nHow many of the 20 stocks look unusual on each measure:")
    for k, c in counts.items():
        print(f"  {k:<12}{c:>3}")
    for name, bad in results.items():
        print(f"{name}: unusual on {len(bad)} of {len(calibrate.TARGETS)} measures {bad}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

It has 500 traders who switch between following fundamentals and following the crowd, and the news that moves the true value is plain bell-curve noise. The script compares the simulated returns with real S&P 500 daily closes from 1950 to today, saved in `data/spx_daily.csv`. Stooq blocks scripted downloads, so I took the same index from Yahoo Finance. Your two checks already show up: with no chartists the returns are bell-curve shaped (kurtosis 0.04), while with herding the tail exponent is 3.3, close to the S&P's 2.9 and the inverse cubic law. Black Monday was a 23-standard-deviation day, and the herding model still produces fewer extreme moves than the real market, so tuning remains. The Lux–Marchesi Nature paper is paywalled, so I downloaded the free Gopikrishnan et al. 1998 inverse-cubic-law preprint to `paper/` instead. """Figures comparing the model with the real market.

Each function draws one figure, saves it, and returns the saved path, so the
same figures can later be reused by the web app.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from scipy.stats import norm

from . import stats


def comparison(real, herd, frac, base, path):
    """2x2 figure: S&P vs model returns, return tails (log-log), chartist share."""
    path = Path(path)
    for name, r in [("real", real), ("herd", herd), ("base", base)]:
        try:
            stats._standardize(r)                  # reject empty/constant/NaN before drawing
        except ValueError as e:
            raise ValueError(f"{name} returns: {e}") from None
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8))
    try:
        _draw_comparison(ax, real, herd, frac, base)
        fig.tight_layout()
        path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        fig.savefig(path, dpi=120)
    finally:
        plt.close(fig)                             # never leave figures open, even on error
    return path


def _draw_comparison(ax, real, herd, frac, base):
    n = min(len(real), len(herd))
    for a, r, title in [(ax[0, 0], real[-n:], f"S&P 500 (last {n} days)"),
                        (ax[0, 1], herd[-n:], f"Model, typical calibrated history (last {n} days)")]:
        a.plot(r / r.std(), lw=0.4, color="#2a6fdb")
        a.set_title(title); a.set_ylabel("return / std"); a.set_ylim(-25, 25)
    a = ax[1, 0]
    for r, lab, c in [(real, "S&P 500", "black"), (herd, "model (calibrated)", "#d94f30"),
                      (base, "no chartists", "#2a6fdb")]:
        z, cc = stats.ccdf(r)
        a.loglog(z, cc, lw=1.5, label=lab, color=c)
    g = np.linspace(1, 8, 100)
    a.loglog(g, 2 * norm.sf(g), "--", color="gray", label="Gaussian")
    a.loglog(g, 0.5 * g ** -3.0, ":", color="green", label="slope -3 (inverse cubic)")
    a.set_ylim(1e-5, 1); a.set_xlim(0.5, 30)
    a.set_xlabel("|return| / std"); a.set_ylabel("P(|r| > x)")
    a.set_title("Tail of the return distribution"); a.legend(fontsize=8)
    ax[1, 1].plot(frac, lw=0.6, color="#7a3fb0")
    ax[1, 1].set_title("Fraction of chartists (herding model)"); ax[1, 1].set_xlabel("day")

def unusual(pct):
    return not 5 <= pct <= 95


def fig_out_of_sample(pool, p, cal_runs):
    """Percentile of each real series among 20 model histories of the same length.
    The 1950- S&P row reuses Fig 1's held-out histories so the two figures agree;
    the 20 stocks are summarized as one row (median percentile, count unusual)."""
    def facts(n, seeds):
        return [stats.stylized_facts(x) for x in ensemble(pool, p, seeds, n)]

    def row(r, sims):
        pct = calibrate.percentiles(stats.stylized_facts(r), sims, calibrate.TARGETS)
        return [pct[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS]

    rows = [row(market_data.spx_returns().values, [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in cal_runs])]
    for i, name in enumerate(["spx_1928", "ndx"]):
        r = market_data.returns(name).values
        rows.append(row(r, facts(len(r), range(700 + 20 * i, 720 + 20 * i))))
    stocks = [market_data.stock_returns(t).values for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
    sims = facts(int(np.median([len(r) for r in stocks])), range(760, 780))
    stock_pct = np.array([row(r, sims) for r in stocks])
    rows.append(np.median(stock_pct, axis=0))
    n_bad = np.sum((stock_pct < 5) | (stock_pct > 95), axis=0)
    m = np.array(rows)
    names = ["S&P 500 1950-2026\n(same histories as Fig 1)", "S&P 500 1928-2026\n(incl. Great Depression)",
             "Nasdaq-100 1985-2026", f"{len(stocks)} stocks, market beta ≈ 1\n(median; # unusual of {len(stocks)})"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.6))
    from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
    cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", ["#256abf", "#9ec5f4", "#f0efec", "#f2a3a2", "#c53a39"])
    im = ax.imshow(m, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(m):
        text = f"{v:.0f}" + (f"\n({n_bad[j]} unusual)" if i == len(m) - 1 else "")
        ax.text(j, i, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK,
                fontweight="bold" if i < len(m) - 1 and unusual(v) else "normal")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(calibrate.TARGETS)), [LABELS[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS],
                  rotation=30, ha="right", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names, fontsize=8.5); ax.grid(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.9, pad=0.02)
    cb.set_label("percentile among 20 model histories\n(50 = typical; <5 or >95 = unusual)", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_title("Fig 6. Out-of-sample: real data the calibration never saw, scored against the model")
    index_bad = int(sum(unusual(v) for v in m[:3].flat))
    save(fig, "fig6_out_of_sample.png",
         f"Each cell is where the real value falls among 20 model histories of the same length (bold = "
         f"unusual). With 10 measures and a 5-95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by chance. "
         f"The three indexes are unusual on {index_bad} of 30 cells. Stocks: {int(n_bad.sum())} of "
         f"{n_bad.size * len(stocks)} stock-measure pairs are unusual; single companies also get "
         f"company-specific news (earnings surprises) that a whole-market model does not have.")
    return m, n_bad

def unusual(pct):
    return not 5 <= pct <= 95


def fig_out_of_sample(pool, p, cal_runs):
    """Percentile of each real series among 20 model histories of the same length.
    The 1950- S&P row reuses Fig 1's held-out histories so the two figures agree;
    the 20 stocks are summarized as one row (median percentile, count unusual)."""
    def facts(n, seeds):
        return [stats.stylized_facts(x) for x in ensemble(pool, p, seeds, n)]

    def row(r, sims):
        pct = calibrate.percentiles(stats.stylized_facts(r), sims, calibrate.TARGETS)
        return [pct[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS]

    rows = [row(market_data.spx_returns().values, [stats.stylized_facts(r) for r in cal_runs])]
    for i, name in enumerate(["spx_1928", "ndx"]):
        r = market_data.returns(name).values
        rows.append(row(r, facts(len(r), range(700 + 20 * i, 720 + 20 * i))))
    stocks = [market_data.stock_returns(t).values for t in market_data.stock_tickers()]
    sims = facts(int(np.median([len(r) for r in stocks])), range(760, 780))
    stock_pct = np.array([row(r, sims) for r in stocks])
    rows.append(np.median(stock_pct, axis=0))
    n_bad = np.sum((stock_pct < 5) | (stock_pct > 95), axis=0)
    m = np.array(rows)
    names = ["S&P 500 1950-2026\n(same histories as Fig 1)", "S&P 500 1928-2026\n(incl. Great Depression)",
             "Nasdaq-100 1985-2026", f"{len(stocks)} stocks, market beta ≈ 1\n(median; # unusual of {len(stocks)})"]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.6))
    from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap
    cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", ["#256abf", "#9ec5f4", "#f0efec", "#f2a3a2", "#c53a39"])
    im = ax.imshow(m, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=100, aspect="auto")
    for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(m):
        text = f"{v:.0f}" + (f"\n({n_bad[j]} unusual)" if i == len(m) - 1 else "")
        ax.text(j, i, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK,
                fontweight="bold" if i < len(m) - 1 and unusual(v) else "normal")
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(calibrate.TARGETS)), [LABELS[k] for k in calibrate.TARGETS],
                  rotation=30, ha="right", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(names)), names, fontsize=8.5); ax.grid(False)
    cb = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.9, pad=0.02)
    cb.set_label("percentile among 20 model histories\n(50 = typical; <5 or >95 = unusual)", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.set_title("Fig 6. Out-of-sample: real data the calibration never saw, scored against the model")
    index_bad = int(sum(unusual(v) for v in m[:3].flat))
    save(fig, "fig6_out_of_sample.png",
         f"Each cell is where the real value falls among 20 model histories of the same length (bold = "
         f"unusual). With 10 measures and a 5-95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by chance. "
         f"The three indexes are unusual on {index_bad} of 30 cells. Stocks: {int(n_bad.sum())} of "
         f"{n_bad.size * len(stocks)} stock-measure pairs are unusual; single companies also get "
         f"company-specific news (earnings surprises) that a whole-market model does not have.")
    return m, n_bad

        off, on = np.expm1(-res[:, 0, j]) * -100, np.expm1(-res[:, 1, j]) * -100
        top = max(off.max(), on.max()) * 1.08
        ax.plot([0, top], [0, top], color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
        ax.scatter(off, on, s=60, color=BLUE, edgecolor="#fcfcfb", linewidth=1.5, zorder=3)

        ax.set_title(f"Circuit breakers: {name}\nlower in {lower}/20 histories, higher in {higher}/20",
                     fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel("fall without breakers (%)"); ax.set_ylabel("fall with breakers (%)")
        ax.set_xlim(0, top); ax.set_ylim(0, top)
        ax.text(0.05 * top, 0.9 * top, "below the line =\nbreakers helped", fontsize=8, color=SECOND)

    shocks = pool.map(_shock_pair, [(p, s) for s in range(5000, 5200)])
    frac = np.array([x[0] for x in shocks])

    bins, names = [(0, 0.1), (0.1, 0.3), (0.3, 1.01)], ["<10%", "10-30%", ">30%"]
    over = [resp[(frac >= lo) & (frac < hi)].max(axis=1) for lo, hi in bins]
    ax = axes[2]
    ax.bar(names, [o.mean() for o in over], color=["#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#184f95"], width=0.55)
    for i, o in enumerate(over):
        ax.plot([i] * len(o), o, "o", color=INK, ms=3, alpha=0.35)
        ax.text(i, o.max() + 0.01, f"n={len(o)}\nmean {o.mean():.2f}×, max {o.max():.2f}×",
                ha="center", fontsize=8.5)
    ax.axhline(1, color=MUTED, ls="--", lw=1.2)
    ax.set_ylim(0.95, max(o.max() for o in over) + 0.09)
    ax.set_xlabel("chartist share when the surprise hits")
    ax.set_ylabel("largest price fall ÷ size of the surprise")
    ax.set_title("A 10% policy surprise: how far the price overshoots\n(1.0 = falls exactly 10%)",
                 fontsize=10)
    fig.suptitle("Fig 7. Policy: breakers soften single days, and surprises hurt most in a crowded market",
                 y=1.05, fontsize=12, fontweight="bold")
    fig.tight_layout()
    save(fig, "fig7_policy.png",
         f"Left and middle: each dot is one 77-year history run twice with identical randomness, without "
         f"and with US-style circuit breakers (15-min pauses at −7% and −13%, close at −20%, scaled "
         f"×{scale:.2f} to the model's volatility); dots on the line are histories where no breaker fired. "
         f"Breakers soften the worst single day but barely change 20-day falls: they spread a crash out "
         f"rather than prevent it. Right: 200 histories run with and without a one-time surprise that cuts "
         f"the value 10% (like an unexpected rate hike). It is amplified only when many chartists are active.")

from pathlib import Path
f = Path("figures/RESULTS.md"); s = f.read_text()
start = s.index("## Fig 6. Out-of-sample"); end = s.index("---\n\n## Honest limitations")
new = """## Fig 6. Out-of-sample test: data the calibration never saw
![](fig6_out_of_sample.png)

**How to read it:** each row is a real data series and each column a measure. A cell is the real data's percentile among 20 model histories of the same length. Pale cells are typical; dark red or blue cells with a bold number are unusual. With 10 measures and a 5–95% band, about 1 unusual cell per row is expected by pure chance.

**Rows:**
- **Top row, for reference:** the 1950–2026 S&P 500 that the model was fitted to. It uses the same 20 held-out histories as Fig 1, so its numbers match Fig 1 exactly. It is *not* out-of-sample.
- **S&P 500 from 1928**, including the 1929 crash and the Great Depression.
- **Nasdaq-100** since 1985.
- **20 stocks with market beta 0.9–1.1** (stocks that move about 1-for-1 with the market), summarized as one row: the median percentile, and how many of the 20 stocks are unusual on that measure.

**Result:**
- The two out-of-sample indexes are unusual on only **1 of 20 cells**: the 1928 S&P's days 2–10 return correlation, the same reversal weak spot as in Fig 1.
- Stocks are unusual on **9 of 200 stock-measure pairs**, all on the short-term return correlations. Single companies also get company-specific news (earnings surprises, lawsuits) that a whole-market model doesn't have.

**Caveats:**
- The stocks are companies that are large *today*, so failed firms are missing (survivorship bias).
- The 2-day reversal is unusual (100%) for the 1950 S&P but only borderline (95%) for the 1928 S&P. An earlier draft scored the 1950 S&P against a different set of 20 histories and got 90%. So the "unusual" verdict depends partly on which random histories you draw.

## Fig 7. Policy experiments: circuit breakers and a policy surprise
![](fig7_policy.png)

Both experiments use **paired runs**: each history is run twice with identical randomness, once with the policy and once without, so any difference is caused by the policy.

**Left and middle, circuit breakers:**
- **Setup:** the real US rules since 2013 are 15-minute pauses at −7% and −13% and a full-day close at −20%. Here they're scaled ×1.34 to match the model's volatility. Dots below the dashed line mean breakers helped; dots exactly on the line are histories where no breaker ever fired.
- **Result:** breakers lower the **worst single day** in 14 of 20 histories. But the **worst 20-day fall** improves in only 11 of 20, close to a coin flip. Pauses **spread a crash over more days rather than prevent it**, because they don't change why traders crowd into trend-following.
- This agrees with the SEC staff's finding that the 1997 halts did not clearly stabilize prices.

**Right, a policy surprise (like an unexpected Fed rate hike):**
- **Setup:** 200 histories, with and without a one-time surprise that cuts the company's true value by 10%. It stands in for real events such as an unexpected rate hike, the 1930 tariffs, or the 2011 US credit downgrade. Histories are grouped by how many chartists were active the day before.
- **Calm market** (under 10% chartists): the price falls almost exactly 10% (mean 1.01×).
- **Crowded market** (over 30% chartists): trend-chasers pile on. The fall overshoots by **7% on average** (a 10% surprise becomes about a 10.7% fall), and by **up to 26%** in the worst case (about a 12.6% fall).
- **In this model, the timing of a policy surprise matters more than its size.**

"""
s = s[:start] + new + s[end:]
s = s.replace("3. **Changes from the 1999 paper.** Log prices, a faster market maker, and minimum group sizes were needed to fix bugs, so the model is not the paper's exact equations.",
 "3. **Changes from the 1999 paper.** Log prices, a faster market maker, and minimum group sizes were needed to fix bugs, so the model is not the paper's exact equations. For example, fundamentalists react to the mispricing |log(value/price)| instead of the paper's |value − price|/price. The two agree for small gaps but differ by a few percent at the 30% mispricings seen in crashes.")

f.write_text(s)
EOF

content.text:
The full test suite is running and takes a few minutes. Here's what I changed while it runs.

**Bugs**

The independent review found **no major bugs** in the model, the statistics, or the calibration. It reran the key numbers in `RESULTS.md` and all of them came out the same. Among other checks:
- the tail-exponent formula gives 3.03 on test data built to have exactly 3;
- the number of traders always adds up to N;
- the calibration and test seeds never overlap.

It found one real bug, which I reproduced myself before fixing:
- **The Kirman ant code accepted impossible settings.** For each step, the chance of an ant moving up plus the chance of moving down must be at most 1. With a large `eps` (spontaneous switching), that sum went over 1, and the simulation disagreed with Kirman's exact answer by 0.2–0.6 (normal is about 0.01). Your figures never used those values, so no results change. The guard in `kirman.py` now rejects those settings, and 4 new tests cover it.

**Figures (now 7 plus `draft.png`)**

| Figure | What changed |
|---|---|

def acf(x, lags):
    x = x - x.mean()
    return np.array([np.corrcoef(x[:-k], x[k:])[0, 1] for k in lags])


def job(args):
    """One simulation -> summary statistics. args = (seed, days, herding, overrides)."""
    seed, days, herding, over = args
    over = dict(over)
    keep = over.pop("keep", False)               # a flag for this script, not a model setting
    base = over.pop("base", model.P)             # start from these settings
    # research script: explore unstable settings too (guard off)
    r, f = model.simulate(days, herding=herding, p=dict(base, **over), seed=seed,
                         max_mispricing=None)
    burn = min(200, days // 10)                  # drop the start-up transient
    r, f = r[burn:], f[burn:]
    return dict(seed=seed, herding=herding, **over,
                kurt=stats.kurtosis(r), alpha=stats.hill_alpha(r), std=r.std(),
                ac1=acf(r, [1])[0], ac1_abs=acf(np.abs(r), [1])[0],
                frac=f.mean(), r=r if keep else None)


def run_all(jobs):
    with Pool() as pool:
        return pd.DataFrame(pool.map(job, jobs))


def main_experiments():
    seeds = range(8)
    spx = pd.read_csv(ROOT / "data/spx_daily.csv", parse_dates=["Date"], index_col="Date")
    real = np.diff(np.log(spx["Close"].values))

    # E1: seed-to-seed variability, herding on vs off
    e1 = run_all([(s, 5000, h, {}) for s in seeds for h in (True, False)])
    # E2: herding strength a1 x chartist trade size tc
    e2 = run_all([(s, 3000, True, dict(a1=a1, tc=tc)) for s in range(3)
                  for a1, tc in product([0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9], [0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2])])
    # E3: time step dt (results should NOT depend on it if the numerics are sound)
    e3 = run_all([(s, 3000, True, dict(dt=dt)) for s in range(4)
                  for dt in [0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1]])
    # E4: number of traders N
    e4 = run_all([(s, 3000, True, dict(N=n)) for s in range(4)
                  for n in [100, 250, 500, 1000, 2000]])
    # E5: price units pf0 (should NOT matter)
    e5 = run_all([(s, 2000, h, dict(pf0=pf)) for s in range(4) for h in (True, False)
                  for pf in [1.0, 10.0, 100.0]])
    # E6: one long run kept for autocorrelation plots
    long_run = job((11, 19600, True, dict(keep=True)))["r"]
    cal_run = job((11, 19600, True, dict(keep=True, base=calibrate.load())))["r"]

    pd.set_option("display.width", 140, "display.precision", 3)
    cols = ["kurt", "alpha", "std", "ac1", "ac1_abs", "frac"]
    print("E1 seeds (mean, std over 8 seeds)\n",
          e1.groupby("herding")[cols].agg(["mean", "std"]).round(3))
    print("\nE2 herding a1 x tc (mean of 3 seeds)\n",
          e2.groupby(["a1", "tc"])[cols].mean().round(3))
    print("\nE3 time step dt\n", e3.groupby("dt")[cols].mean().round(4))
    print("\nE4 traders N\n", e4.groupby("N")[cols].mean().round(3))
    print("\nE5 price units pf0\n", e5.groupby(["herding", "pf0"])[cols].mean().round(4))
    print(f"\nS&P 500: kurt={stats.kurtosis(real):.2f} alpha={stats.hill_alpha(real):.2f} "
          f"ac1={acf(real, [1])[0]:.3f} ac1_abs={acf(np.abs(real), [1])[0]:.3f}")

    # ---- Figures
    FIG.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
    for i, (col, ref, lab) in enumerate([("kurt", stats.kurtosis(real), "S&P 500"),
                                          ("alpha", stats.hill_alpha(real), "S&P 500")]):
        for h, c in [(True, "#d94f30"), (False, "#2a6fdb")]:
            v = e1[e1.herding == h][col]
            ax[i].scatter(np.full(len(v), int(h)) + np.random.default_rng(0).uniform(-.1, .1, len(v)),
                          v, color=c, label="herding" if h else "no chartists")
        ax[i].axhline(ref, color="black", ls="--", label=lab)
        ax[i].set_xticks([0, 1], ["no chartists", "herding"])
        ax[i].set_title(["Excess kurtosis (0 = bell curve)", "Tail exponent α (S&P ≈ 3)"][i])
    ax[0].set_yscale("symlog"); ax[1].legend(fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle("E1: 8 random seeds, 5000 days each")
    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(FIG / "test_seeds.png", dpi=110)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 4))
    for a, col, title in zip(ax, ["alpha", "kurt", "frac"],
                             ["Tail exponent α", "Excess kurtosis", "Mean chartist fraction"]):
        g = e2.groupby(["a1", "tc"])[col].mean().unstack()
        im = a.imshow(g.values, origin="lower", cmap="viridis", aspect="auto")
        a.set_xticks(range(len(g.columns)), g.columns); a.set_yticks(range(len(g.index)), g.index)
        a.set_xlabel("tc (chartist trade size)"); a.set_ylabel("a1 (herding strength)")
        for (i, j), v in np.ndenumerate(g.values):
            a.text(j, i, f"{v:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=8)
        a.set_title(title); fig.colorbar(im, ax=a)
    fig.suptitle("E2: parameter grid (3 seeds each)")
    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(FIG / "test_param_grid.png", dpi=110)

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.6))
    for a, (df, key, title) in zip(ax, [(e3, "dt", "E3: time step dt"), (e4, "N", "E4: traders N"),
                                        (e5[e5.herding], "pf0", "E5: price units pf0 (herding)"),
                                        (e5[~e5.herding], "pf0", "E5: price units pf0 (no chartists)")]):
        m = df.groupby(key)[["alpha", "kurt"]].mean()
        sd = df.groupby(key)["std"].mean() / df["std"].mean()
        a.plot(m.index, m["alpha"], "o-", label="α")
        a.plot(m.index, m["kurt"], "s-", label="kurtosis")
        a.plot(m.index, sd, "^-", label="return std (relative)")
        a.set_xscale("log"); a.set_xlabel(key); a.set_title(title); a.legend(fontsize=7)
    fig.suptitle("Should these be flat? dt and pf0: yes. N: the paper says effects fade as N grows.")
    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(FIG / "test_sensitivity.png", dpi=110)

    lags = np.arange(1, 101)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
    for r, lab, c in [(real, "S&P 500", "black"), (long_run, "model (paper set)", "#d94f30"),
                      (cal_run, "model (calibrated)", "#2a9d4b")]:
        ax[0].plot(lags[:20], acf(r, lags[:20]), "o-", ms=3, label=lab, color=c)
        ax[1].plot(lags, acf(np.abs(r), lags), lw=1.5, label=lab, color=c)
    for a in ax: a.axhline(0, color="gray", lw=0.5); a.legend()
    ax[0].set_title("Autocorrelation of returns (real: ≈ 0)")
    ax[1].set_title("Autocorrelation of |returns| (volatility clustering)")
    ax[1].set_xlabel("lag (days)"); ax[0].set_xlabel("lag (days)")
    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(FIG / "test_autocorrelation.png", dpi=110)

    tails = [0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1]
    g = np.random.default_rng(0).standard_normal(len(real))
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
    for r, lab, c in [(real, "S&P 500", "black"), (long_run, "model (paper set)", "#d94f30"),
                      (cal_run, "model (calibrated)", "#2a9d4b"),
                      (g, "Gaussian", "gray")]:
        ax.plot(tails, [stats.hill_alpha(r, t) for t in tails], "o-", label=lab, color=c)
    ax.axhline(3, ls=":", color="green", label="inverse cubic (3)")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("fraction of data used as 'tail'"); ax.set_ylabel("Hill α")
    ax.set_title("How much does α depend on the tail cut?"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
    fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig(FIG / "test_hill_tail_choice.png", dpi=110)
    print("\nSaved figures/diagnostics/test_*.png")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main_experiments()

"""Lux-Marchesi (1999) agent-based market model, with guardrails.

N traders are fundamentalists (buy below the fundamental value, sell above) or
chartists: optimists (buy) and pessimists (sell) who follow the crowd and the
trend, Kirman-style. Traders switch groups by comparing profits, and every
switch is a recruitment: the more members a group has, the faster it grows.
News moves the fundamental value with plain Gaussian noise.

Prices are logs, so only *relative* mispricing matters. The inner loop runs
under numba when it is installed (about 20x faster) and as plain Python
otherwise; both use the same random numbers and give identical results.
"""
import os
import warnings

import numpy as np

try:
    import numba
except ImportError:                       # e.g. a web host without numba
    numba = None

# Parameters after Lux & Marchesi (2000), rewritten in log-price units so the
# model does not depend on the price level (pf0 only sets the starting price).
P = dict(N=500, v1=3.0, v2=2.0, beta=50.0, tc=0.1, gamma=0.1,
         a1=0.6, a2=2.0, a3=0.5, R=0.0004, s=0.75, sigma_news=0.01,
         pf0=10.0, dt=0.02, min_chartists=4, tau=0.2)

U_MAX = 30.0           # cap on switching exponents (prevents overflow)
N_STABLE = 250         # below this the price swings wildly (tested)
MAX_MISPRICING = 1.0   # healthy runs stay below 0.6 (measured); runaways reach 5-16
POSITIVE = ("v1", "v2", "beta", "gamma", "tc", "sigma_news", "tau", "pf0", "dt")
NON_NEGATIVE = ("a1", "a2", "a3", "s", "R")
WHOLE = ("N", "min_chartists")


class ModelRegimeError(RuntimeError):
    """The simulated market left the range where the model is meaningful."""


# ------------------------------------------------------------------ guardrails

def check_settings(p):
    """Every setting present, spelled right, a finite number, with a sensible sign."""
    unknown, missing = set(p) - set(P), set(P) - set(p)
    if unknown:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown setting(s) {sorted(unknown)} -- typo? valid: {sorted(P)}")
    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"missing setting(s) {sorted(missing)}")
    for key, v in p.items():
        if isinstance(v, bool) or not isinstance(v, (int, float, np.number)) or not np.isfinite(v):
            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be a finite number, got {v!r}")
        if key in POSITIVE and v <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be > 0, got {v}")
        if key in NON_NEGATIVE and v < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be >= 0, got {v}")
        if key in WHOLE and float(v) != int(v):
            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be a whole number, got {v}")


def check_inputs(days, herding, p):
    """Raise ValueError for inputs that would give silently wrong results."""
    check_settings(p)
    if days < 0 or int(days) != days:
        raise ValueError(f"days must be a whole number >= 0, got {days}")
    dt = p["dt"]
    if round(1 / dt) < 1 or abs(round(1 / dt) * dt - 1) > 1e-9:
        raise ValueError(f"dt must divide one day exactly (e.g. 0.01, 0.02, 0.05), got {dt}")
    if dt > 1 / (p["beta"] * p["gamma"]) + 1e-12:
        raise ValueError(f"dt={dt} breaks stability: price would overshoot; "
                         f"need dt <= 1/(beta*gamma) = {1 / (p['beta'] * p['gamma']):.3g}")
    m = p["min_chartists"]
    if herding:
        if m < 2 or m % 2:
            raise ValueError(f"min_chartists must be even and >= 2, got {m}")
        if p["N"] < 10 * m:
            raise ValueError(f"N={p['N']} is too small: need N >= {10 * m} "

        if p["N"] < N_STABLE:

"""Lux-Marchesi (1999) agent-based market model, with guardrails.

N traders are fundamentalists (buy below the fundamental value, sell above) or
chartists: optimists (buy) and pessimists (sell) who follow the crowd and the
trend, Kirman-style. Traders switch groups by comparing profits, and every
switch is a recruitment: the more members a group has, the faster it grows.
News moves the fundamental value with plain Gaussian noise.

Prices are logs, so only *relative* mispricing matters. The inner loop runs
under numba when it is installed (about 20x faster) and as plain Python
otherwise; both use the same random numbers and give identical results.

import warnings

import numpy as np

# model does not depend on the price level (pf0 only sets the starting price).

         a1=0.6, a2=2.0, a3=0.5, R=0.0004, s=0.75, sigma_news=0.01,
         pf0=10.0, dt=0.02, min_chartists=4, tau=0.2)

POSITIVE = ("v1", "v2", "beta", "gamma", "tc", "sigma_news", "tau", "pf0", "dt")
NON_NEGATIVE = ("a1", "a2", "a3", "s", "R")
WHOLE = ("N", "min_chartists")


class ModelRegimeError(RuntimeError):
    """The simulated market left the range where the model is meaningful."""

    if missing:
        raise ValueError(f"missing setting(s) {sorted(missing)}")
    for key, v in p.items():
        if isinstance(v, bool) or not isinstance(v, (int, float, np.number)) or not np.isfinite(v):
            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be a finite number, got {v!r}")
        if key in POSITIVE and v <= 0:
            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be > 0, got {v}")
        if key in NON_NEGATIVE and v < 0:

            raise ValueError(f"setting {key} must be a whole number, got {v}")

halts = np.zeros(days, dtype=np.int64)     # 0 none, 1-2 pauses, 3 closed for the day
    low = np.empty(days)                       # lowest log price vs previous close
    max_step = 0.0
    out_lp[0] = lp
    out_lf[0] = lf
    for day in range(days):
        lf += shock[day]                       # policy surprise (0 on ordinary days)
        prev_close = lp
        day_low = 0.0
        paused = 0                             # steps of pause left
        closed = False
        for _ in range(steps):
            if herding:
                nc = npl + nmi
                # optimist <-> pessimist: herding (a1 * opinion) + trend (a2)
                U1 = _clip(a1 * (npl - nmi) / nc + a2 * trend / v1)
                rate = v1 * nc / N * dt
                up = min(g.binomial(nmi, _prob(rate * np.exp(U1))), nmi - m2)
                down = min(g.binomial(npl, _prob(rate * np.exp(-U1))), npl - m2)
                npl, nmi = npl + up - down, nmi - up + down
                # chartist <-> fundamentalist: compare expected profits
                mis = abs(lf - lp)                       # relative mispricing
                yld = R * np.exp(min(lf - lp, U_MAX))    # dividend yield
                U21 = _clip(a3 * (yld + trend / v2 - R - s * mis))
                U22 = _clip(a3 * (R - yld - trend / v2 - s * mis))
                r2 = v2 * dt / N
                # floors: someone must remain in every group, or nobody could
                # ever be recruited back into it (Kirman-style switching)
                f2o = min(g.binomial(nf, _prob(r2 * npl * np.exp(U21))), nf - mF)
                f2p = min(g.binomial(nf - f2o, _prob(r2 * nmi * np.exp(U22))), nf - f2o - mF)
                o2f = min(g.binomial(npl, _prob(r2 * nf * np.exp(-U21))), npl - m2)
                p2f = min(g.binomial(nmi, _prob(r2 * nf * np.exp(-U22))), nmi - m2)
                npl += f2o - o2f
                nmi += f2p - p2f
                nf += o2f + p2f - f2o - f2p
            # market maker: log price moves with excess demand (frozen while halted)
            if closed or paused > 0:
                dlp = 0.0
                paused = max(0, paused - 1)
            else:
                ed = (npl - nmi) * tc + nf * gamma * (lf - lp)
                dlp = beta * ed / N * dt
            lp += dlp
            trend += (dlp / dt - trend) * min(1.0, dt / tau)   # smoothed
            max_step = max(max_step, abs(dlp))
            fall = lp - prev_close
            day_low = min(day_low, fall)
            # circuit breakers: each level fires at most once a day
            if cb3 < 0 and not closed and fall <= cb3:
                closed = True
                halts[day] = 3
            elif cb2 < 0 and halts[day] < 2 and fall <= cb2:
                halts[day] = 2
                paused = halt_steps
            elif cb1 < 0 and halts[day] < 1 and fall <= cb1:
                halts[day] = 1
                paused = halt_steps
            # Gaussian news moves the fundamental value
            lf += sigma * np.sqrt(dt) * g.standard_normal()
        out_lp[day + 1] = lp
        out_lf[day + 1] = lf
        frac[day] = (npl + nmi) / N
        low[day] = day_low
        if not np.isfinite(lp):
            return out_lp, out_lf, frac, halts, low, max_step, 1, day
        if max_mis > 0 and abs(lp - lf) > max_mis:
            return out_lp, out_lf, frac, halts, low, max_step, 2, day

def check_breakers(breakers):
    """Circuit-breaker rules: dict(levels=(l1, l2, l3), halt_minutes=m), where the
    levels are price falls below the previous close (e.g. 0.07 = 7%), increasing,
    and l1, l2 pause trading for m minutes of a 390-minute day; l3 closes the day."""
    if breakers is None:
        return
    if set(breakers) != {"levels", "halt_minutes"}:
        raise ValueError(f"breakers needs exactly 'levels' and 'halt_minutes', got {sorted(breakers)}")
    lv = tuple(breakers["levels"])
    if len(lv) != 3 or not all(0 < x < 1 for x in lv) or not lv[0] < lv[1] < lv[2]:
        raise ValueError(f"breakers levels must be 3 increasing falls between 0 and 1, got {lv}")
    if not breakers["halt_minutes"] > 0:
        raise ValueError(f"breakers halt_minutes must be > 0, got {breakers['halt_minutes']}")

    """Policy shocks: {day: fractional change of the fundamental value}, e.g.
    {200: -0.05} = on day 200 a surprise cuts the value by 5%."""
    for day, x in (shocks or {}).items():
        if isinstance(day, bool) or not isinstance(day, (int, np.integer)) or not 0 <= day < days:
            raise ValueError(f"shock day must be a whole number from 0 to {days - 1}, got {day!r}")
        if isinstance(x, bool) or not isinstance(x, (int, float, np.number)) or not np.isfinite(x) \
                or x <= -1:
            raise ValueError(f"shock on day {day} must be a number > -1 (a fraction), got {x!r}")


def simulate_full(days, herding=True, p=P, seed=None, max_mispricing=MAX_MISPRICING,
                  breakers=None, shocks=None):

    r (daily log returns), frac (chartist share at each close), lp, lf (log price
    and log value, days + 1 values), halts (0 none, 1-2 pause levels, 3 closed),
    low (each day's lowest log price vs the previous close), max_step (largest
    one-step log price move). See simulate() for the guardrails."""
    check_inputs(days, herding, p)
    check_breakers(breakers)
    check_shocks(shocks, days)
    shock = np.zeros(int(days))
    for day, x in (shocks or {}).items():
        shock[day] += np.log1p(x)
    N, steps = int(p["N"]), int(round(1 / p["dt"]))
    m = int(p["min_chartists"])
    nf, npl, nmi = initial_counts(N, herding, m)
    if breakers is None:
        cb, halt_steps = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0
    else:
        cb = tuple(float(np.log(1 - x)) for x in breakers["levels"])
        halt_steps = max(1, int(round(breakers["halt_minutes"] / 390 * steps)))
    lp, lf, frac, halts, low, max_step, status, day = _run(
        np.random.default_rng(seed), int(days), steps, bool(herding), N, nf, npl, nmi,
        m // 2 if herding else 0, m, float(np.log(p["pf0"])),
        *(float(p[k]) for k in ("v1", "v2", "beta", "tc", "gamma", "a1", "a2", "a3",
                                "R", "s", "sigma_news", "tau")),
        -1.0 if max_mispricing is None else float(max_mispricing), *cb, halt_steps, shock)
    if status == 1:
        raise FloatingPointError("simulation diverged; try a smaller dt")
    if status == 2:
        gap = abs(lp[day + 1] - lf[day + 1])
        raise ModelRegimeError(
            f"day {day}: price is {np.exp(gap):.1f}x away from its value "
            f"with {frac[day]:.0%} chartists. These settings are outside the "
            f"model's realistic range (known causes: N < {N_STABLE}, s < 0.5, v2 < 1). "
            f"Pass max_mispricing=None to run anyway.")
    return dict(r=np.diff(lp), frac=frac, lp=lp, lf=lf, halts=halts, low=low,
                max_step=float(max_step))


def simulate(days, herding=True, p=P, seed=None, paths=False,
             max_mispricing=MAX_MISPRICING, breakers=None, shocks=None):
    """Simulate the market for `days` trading days.

    Returns daily log returns and the chartist fraction at each day's close;
    with paths=True also the daily log price and log fundamental value.

    o = simulate_full(days, herding, p, seed, max_mispricing, breakers, shocks)
    return (o["r"], o["frac"], o["lp"], o["lf"]) if paths else (o["r"], o["frac"])

# Stocks matched by market beta

Daily closing prices, 2000 to today, from Yahoo Finance (`yfinance`, `auto_adjust=False`).
Prices are **split-adjusted but not dividend-adjusted**, the same as the S&P 500 and
Nasdaq-100 index files, so all returns are measured the same way.

`market_beta.csv` lists each stock's market beta: the slope of its daily log return

market moves 1%. The 20 stocks were chosen from about 80 large companies with full
price history since 2000, keeping those with beta between 0.9 and 1.1.

Caveat (survivorship bias): the candidates are companies that are large today, so
firms that failed or shrank since 2000 are missing.
